# TidyByte — Full Site Content

Download on the App Store: https://apps.apple.com/in/app/tidybyte/id6775769763

## Homepage

TidyByte — Swipe to clean your photos.

Free up storage in minutes. Swipe to delete junk photos, find duplicates and blurry shots, and compress videos — all 100% on your device. No ads, no account.

### Trust Signals

- 100% on-device processing
- No ads
- No account required
- Free forever

### How It Works

TidyByte turns photo cleanup into something you'll actually finish. Swipe left to delete, swipe right to keep — and reclaim gigabytes in minutes.

1. Swipe left to delete. A subtle haptic tap confirms the throw. Undo is always one tap away.
2. A deck of photos. Every review feels like flipping through a familiar stack.
3. Swipe right to keep. Saved photos flow straight to an album you pick, ready to revisit.

### Cleanup Toolkit

Beyond swiping, TidyByte packs a full toolkit of smart cleanup tools — all on-device:

- **Duplicates**: Find exact copies, byte-for-byte. Exact duplicates are matched by SHA-256 hash of the file data.
- **Similar photos**: Group near-identical shots. Near-duplicates use Apple Vision feature prints to find visually similar shots.
- **Screenshots**: Round up and clear them in one pass.
- **Blurry photos**: Spot out-of-focus and shaky shots.
- **Large files**: Surface the biggest space hogs.
- **Burst photos**: Pick the best from a sequence.
- **Live Photos**: Convert to stills to save space.
- **Video compression**: Shrink videos, keep them watchable.
- **Photo compression**: Re-encode photos to reclaim space.
- **Smart Categories**: Sort by content type, browse faster.

### Privacy Promise

Your photos never leave your phone.

- All processing happens on-device using Apple's Photos and Vision frameworks.
- No backend, no analytics, no third-party scripts, no tracking — anywhere.
- We can't see your photos. We don't want to.

### Storage Dashboard

A live donut chart of where your storage goes — photos, videos, screenshots, Live Photos, other. Tappable slices drill into the exact items you can free up.

### Activity & Savings

Track your progress: total space freed, how many items you've cleaned, a 30-day chart, and a per-tool breakdown of where the savings came from. Space freed by cleaning items stored only in iCloud isn't counted, so the total is a floor rather than an estimate.

### Widget and Shortcuts

A Home Screen widget shows storage used, what's reclaimable, and how much you've freed so far, with buttons that jump straight into a swipe session or the screenshot cleaner. Siri and the Shortcuts app can answer "how much can I free up?" without opening the app, or launch any cleanup tool directly.

### Open Source

TidyByte is MIT-licensed. Read the source, verify the claims, file an issue. GitHub: https://github.com/360ghar/snap-clean-ios

### Frequently Asked Questions

**Does TidyByte upload my photos?**
No. All processing happens locally on your iPhone using Apple's Photos and Vision frameworks. TidyByte has no backend, no analytics SDK, and no tracking.

**What about iCloud-only photos?**
TidyByte works with your full library, including assets stored only in iCloud. The system downloads them as needed; you can also swipe past without waiting.

**Are deleted photos gone immediately?**
They go to the iOS Recently Deleted album, where they sit for 30 days before being permanently removed — exactly like deleting from the Photos app.

**Will it lower the quality of my photos?**
No cleanup tool touches the originals. The only operation that re-encodes is the explicit Video Compression or Photo Compression tool, and you choose the preset.

**How are duplicates detected?**
Exact duplicates are matched by SHA-256 hash of the file data. Near-duplicates use Apple Vision feature prints to find visually similar shots.

**Is there a free trial or subscription?**
TidyByte is free, with no in-app purchases and no paywalls. Every feature is available to every user.

**Does TidyByte support iPad?**
Yes. TidyByte is a universal app that runs natively on iPhone and iPad. Every cleanup tool works on both, the swipe interface adapts to the iPad's larger screen, and iPad supports all orientations.

**How do I report a bug or request a feature?**
Open an issue on GitHub (https://github.com/360ghar/snap-clean-ios) or use the contact form on the Support page.

---

## Privacy Policy

Effective: January 1, 2026.

TidyByte is 100% on-device. We collect no data from you. No photos, no usage analytics, no personal information, no crash reports with PII. The app has no backend server, no analytics SDK, and no third-party dependencies that could transmit data. All photo analysis and processing uses Apple's built-in Photos and Vision frameworks on your device.

Permissions requested: Photo Library (read & write) — required for the app to function. Notifications — optional, only for cleanup reminders.

Data storage: TidyByte stores local records (SwipeRecord, CompressionRecord, StorageSnapshot) using SwiftData in a sandboxed database on your phone. This data never leaves your device and can be cleared via Settings → Reset Swipe History.

Read the full privacy policy at https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/privacy.

## Are Photo Cleaner Apps Safe? Privacy Guide | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/are-photo-cleaner-apps-safe

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Are Photo Cleaner Apps Safe? Privacy Are Photo Cleaner Apps Safe? What to Look For Your photo library is one of the most personal things on your phone. Before you hand access to any cleaning app, you need to know what it does with your images, where they go, and who can see them. This guide breaks down the real risks and shows you exactly how to evaluate whether a photo cleaner app is safe. June 13, 2026 &middot; 8 min read What Permissions Photo Cleaner Apps Request When you install a photo cleaner app on your iPhone, the first thing it asks for is access to your photo library. This is expected — the app cannot function without seeing your images. But the scope of that access matters. On iOS 14 and later, Apple gives you two options: grant access to your entire library or limit it to selected photos. A well-designed app works with either choice, though full access produces better results for features like duplicate detection and blur analysis. Beyond photo access, some apps request additional permissions that deserve scrutiny. Network access is the big one. A photo cleaner has no inherent reason to connect to the internet, yet many popular apps do exactly that. They may send analytics data, load advertisements, or upload photos to remote servers for processing. Other permissions to watch for include access to your contacts, location data, and microphone — none of which are necessary for cleaning your photo library. The safest apps keep their permission footprint minimal. They ask only for photo library access and nothing else. If an app requests network, camera, contacts, or location permissions, that is a red flag worth investigating before you proceed. You can always check and revoke permissions later in your iPhone's Settings app under Privacy and Security, but it is better to evaluate an app's behavior before you grant access in the first place. The Risk: Apps That Upload to Cloud Servers The single biggest privacy risk with photo cleaner apps is cloud processing. When an app uploads your photos to remote servers for analysis, your images leave your device and enter someone else's infrastructure. Even if the company claims to delete photos after processing, you have no way to verify that claim. Your photos transit the open internet, sit temporarily on a server you do not control, and may be cached in logs or backups you will never see. A 2024 analysis by the Electronic Frontier Foundation found that over 60 percent of top-ranking photo utility apps on the App Store transmitted user images to external servers. Some did so for legitimate machine learning purposes, but many sent photos to advertising and analytics third parties. In several documented cases, apps that claimed "on-device processing" in their marketing materials were caught uploading thumbnails or compressed copies to their own servers. Cloud processing also introduces data breach risk. Any server connected to the internet can be compromised. If a photo cleaning service stores even temporary copies of your images on its servers, a breach could expose your private photos. The consequences range from embarrassment to targeted phishing to identity theft, depending on what is in your library. On-device processing eliminates this entire category of risk because your photos never leave your phone. For most users wondering if photo cleaner apps are safe, the answer hinges on whether that app ever sends your images off-device. How to Verify an App Is Truly On-Device Marketing claims are cheap. An app can say "100% private" on its landing page and still phone home in the background. Here is how to verify whether a photo cleaner actually processes images locally. Check the App Store Privacy Label Every app on the App Store has a privacy nutrition label that discloses what data it collects and whether that data is linked to your identity. Scroll to the "App Privacy" section on the app's listing. If you see "Photos" or "Videos" listed under "Data Linked to You" or "Data Used to Track You," the app uploads your images. A truly on-device app should show minimal or no data collection in these categories. Monitor Network Activity Tools like Charles Proxy, mitmproxy, or a firewall app such as Lockdown Privacy can show you exactly which servers an app contacts while running. Install the tool, launch the photo cleaner, and observe the network traffic. If the app sends data to cloud endpoints — especially large payloads consistent with image uploads — it is not truly on-device. Be aware that some apps only upload periodically or under specific conditions, so test with different actions like scanning, reviewing, and deleting. Read the Source Code Open-source apps offer the strongest transparency guarantee. When the source code is publicly available, security researchers and privacy advocates can audit every line for network calls, data exfiltration, and tracking. If you are not a developer, look for community discussions, blog posts, or third-party audits that vouch for the app's behavior. Closed-source apps require you to trust the developer's word, which is a weaker privacy posture. TidyByte's Approach: Open Source, No Backend TidyByte was built from the ground up to answer the question "are photo cleaner apps safe?" with a definitive yes. Every piece of processing happens on your iPhone or iPad using Apple's native frameworks. The app uses the Vision framework for blur detection and image analysis, PhotoKit for library operations, and AVFoundation for video compression. None of these require network access, and TidyByte never opens a network connection for any processing task. TidyByte's Privacy Guarantees No backend servers. TidyByte has no server infrastructure. There is nowhere for your photos to be uploaded even if the app tried. No user accounts. You never create a login, provide an email, or give any identifying information. There is no user database. No analytics or tracking. TidyByte does not include any analytics SDK, advertising framework, or tracking pixel. Your usage patterns are your own. Fully open source. The entire codebase is published under the MIT license on GitHub . Anyone can audit it. No third-party dependencies. The app is built exclusively with Apple frameworks. There are no CocoaPods, Swift Packages, or external libraries that could introduce hidden tracking. This architecture means TidyByte's privacy is not a policy promise — it is a technical guarantee. The app cannot upload your photos because there is no server to receive them. It cannot track you because there is no analytics endpoint. It cannot leak data through a dependency because it has none. If you are looking for a photo cleaner that is provably safe, TidyByte's open-source, zero-network design is as strong as it gets. Checklist for Evaluating Any Photo App's Privacy Before you install any photo cleaner — or any app that requests access to your personal data — run through this checklist. Each item represents a concrete privacy signal you can verify in minutes. Check What to Look For Red Flag Privacy Label Photos not listed under collected data Photos or Videos in "Data Linked to You" Network Access No internet connection required App fails or shows errors when offline Source Code Public repository on GitHub or similar Closed source with no audit reports Account Requirement Works without creating an account Requires email, phone, or social login Permissions Only requests photo library access Requests contacts, location, microphone Third-Party SDKs No ads, analytics, or tracking frameworks Facebook SDK, Google Analytics, Firebase An app that passes every row in this table is about as private as software can get. Very few photo cleaners on the App Store meet all six criteria. TidyByte does, which is why it stands out as the privacy-first choice for users who want to clean their photo library without compromising their data. App Store Privacy Labels Explained Apple introduced privacy nutrition labels in December 2020 to give users a quick overview of how apps handle data. Every app must disclose what data it collects, how that data is used, and whether it is linked to your identity. Understanding these labels is essential when evaluating whether photo cleaner apps are safe. The Three Categories Privacy labels are divided into three tiers. "Data Used to Track You" is the most invasive — it means the app shares your data with third-party advertising or data broker networks. "Data Linked to You" means the app collects data tied to your identity through your account, device ID, or other identifiers. "Data Not Linked to You" means the app collects data but in an anonymized or aggregated form that cannot be traced back to you personally. What to Watch For With Photo Apps For a photo cleaning app specifically, look at whether "Photos" appears under any of the three categories. If photos are listed under "Data Used to Track You," delete the app immediately — that means your images are being shared with advertisers. If photos appear under "Data Linked to You," the app uploads your images and ties them to your identity. Neither scenario is acceptable for a privacy-conscious user. Also pay attention to "Other Data" categories. Some apps avoid listing "Photos" explicitly but still upload image metadata, thumbnails, or hashes to their servers. The privacy label is self-reported by developers and is not independently audited by Apple, so it should be treated as a useful starting point rather than a complete guarantee. Combine it with the other verification methods in this guide — especially source code review for open-source apps like TidyByte — to build a complete picture of an app's privacy behavior. Frequently Asked Questions Are photo cleaner apps safe to use? Photo cleaner apps can be safe, but it depends entirely on how they handle your data. Apps that process photos locally on your device without uploading them to remote servers are the safest option. Always check the app's privacy policy, App Store privacy label, and whether the source code is publicly available before granting access to your photo library. Do photo cleaner apps access all my photos? Most photo cleaner apps request full access to your photo library because they need to scan and analyze your images to identify duplicates, screenshots, and other cleanup candidates. On iOS, you can grant limited access to selected photos instead, though this may reduce the app's effectiveness. Apps like TidyByte respect whichever permission level you choose and never request access beyond what is needed. How do I know if an app uploads my photos? You can check an app's App Store privacy label under the "Data Linked to You" section — if it lists Photos or Videos as data collected and transmitted, the app likely uploads your images. You can also monitor network activity using tools like Charles Proxy or Little Snitch. Open-source apps are the most transparent because their code can be independently audited for any network calls. Is TidyByte safe for my private photos? Yes. TidyByte processes all photos entirely on your device using Apple's Vision framework and native iOS APIs. It has no backend server, no user accounts, and no analytics that track your behavior. The app is fully open source under the MIT license, so anyone can inspect the code to verify that no data ever leaves your device. What should I look for in a privacy-focused photo app? Look for four key indicators: on-device processing with no cloud uploads, a transparent App Store privacy label showing minimal data collection, open-source code that can be independently audited, and no requirement to create an account. Apps that meet all four criteria — like TidyByte — give you the strongest privacy guarantees without sacrificing functionality. Ready to clean up your photo library? TidyByte is free, runs 100% on your device, and takes just minutes to use. Download TidyByte Free See all features TidyByte Swipe to clean your photos. ## Best Free Alternative to CleanMyPhone | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/best-alternative-to-cleanmyphone

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Best Free Alternative to CleanMyPhone Comparison Best Free Alternative to CleanMyPhone for iPhone CleanMyPhone is one of the better-known photo cleanup apps on the App Store. It finds duplicates, flags blurry shots, and helps you reclaim storage. But it costs $30 to $45 per year — and every feature it offers is available for free. TidyByte is a free alternative to CleanMyPhone that does the same job without a subscription, without an account, and without ever touching your photos on a remote server. What CleanMyPhone Offers CleanMyPhone markets itself as an all-in-one storage cleaner for iPhone and iPad. Its feature set covers the essentials most people need when their device runs low on space. At its core, the app scans your photo library and surfaces media that you are likely to delete — duplicates, blurry photos, overexposed or underexposed shots, and screenshots you have already read. Beyond basic scanning, CleanMyPhone includes a duplicate video finder, a contacts cleaner, and some organizational tools like photo grouping by date or location. It presents results in a card-style interface where you swipe or tap to confirm deletions. The app also estimates how much storage you will recover, which gives users a concrete motivation to keep cleaning. On paper, this is a solid feature list. The problem is not what CleanMyPhone does — it is what it charges for doing it. Every feature listed above has a free, on-device implementation available through open-source tools. You do not need to pay a yearly subscription to find duplicate photos on your own phone. The underlying iOS frameworks — PhotoKit, Vision, AVFoundation — already provide everything needed to build these features, which is exactly what TidyByte does. What CleanMyPhone Costs CleanMyPhone uses a subscription model. Depending on the plan, you will pay somewhere between $30 and $45 per year for access to its features. Some plans offer a lower first-year promotional rate, but once the trial ends, the full price kicks in automatically unless you cancel. That means over three years of use, you are looking at roughly $90 to $135 spent on an app whose primary function is deleting files you do not need. There is an important nuance worth understanding here: CleanMyPhone runs its analysis on your device, but it also connects to external servers for certain operations. That combination of subscription pricing and server-side processing raises two concerns. First, you are paying for compute that your own iPhone can handle. Second, your photo data — or at least metadata about your photos — passes through infrastructure you do not control. For privacy-conscious users, that is a meaningful trade-off. To put the cost in perspective, the average iPhone user accumulates roughly 5 to 10 GB of redundant photos and videos per year. A single cleanup session with a free tool like TidyByte can recover that same space. Paying $30 or more annually to delete files from your own device is a hard value proposition to justify when the alternative costs nothing. If you are evaluating whether a subscription makes sense, it helps to know exactly what you get for free. TidyByte: The Same Features for Free TidyByte is an open-source iOS app built specifically to do what CleanMyPhone does — without charging anything. It uses the same Apple frameworks under the hood: PhotoKit for library access, Vision for blur and exposure detection, AVFoundation for video compression, and SHA-256 hashing for exact duplicate identification. The result is a tool that matches CleanMyPhone's core feature set while remaining completely free. The app runs a swipe-based interface that makes cleanup fast and almost effortless. You see one photo at a time, swipe left to delete or right to keep, and the app handles the rest. This pattern works because it turns a tedious chore — scrolling through thousands of photos looking for bad ones — into a quick, almost game-like experience. Most users clear out hundreds of photos in a single session without feeling overwhelmed. As a free alternative to CleanMyPhone, TidyByte does not compromise on capability. It identifies exact duplicates using file-level hashing, detects near-duplicates through Apple's Vision framework, flags blurry and poorly exposed photos, surfaces large videos that are candidates for compression, and highlights old screenshots. There is no feature gating, no premium tier, and no paywall. Every tool is available the moment you install the app. You can read more about the full feature set on the TidyByte features page . This is not a marketing summary — it is a direct feature-to-feature match based on what each app actually delivers. Privacy Comparison When you install a photo cleanup app, you are granting it access to your entire photo library — every image, every video, every screenshot. That makes privacy a critical factor, not a secondary concern. Here is how the two apps differ on the privacy front. TidyByte processes every photo and video directly on your iPhone. No image data, no metadata, no file hashes, and no usage analytics leave your device. The app has no backend server, no user accounts, and no tracking of any kind. Because it is fully open source under the MIT license, anyone can inspect the code to verify these claims. You do not have to trust a privacy policy — you can read the source code itself on GitHub . CleanMyPhone, by contrast, uses a mix of on-device and server-side processing. While the core scanning happens locally, certain features rely on cloud infrastructure. The app also requires an account to function, which ties your usage to an identity. For a tool that exists solely to manage your personal photos, that level of data exposure is worth thinking about. According to Apple's own privacy guidelines , the best apps process data on-device whenever possible — and that is exactly what TidyByte does. If privacy matters to you, the choice between a closed-source subscription app and a free, open-source, on-device alternative is not a close call. How to Switch from CleanMyPhone to TidyByte Switching from CleanMyPhone to TidyByte takes less than five minutes. There is no data to migrate, no account to transfer, and no settings to reconfigure. Here is the exact process: Step 1: Cancel your CleanMyPhone subscription. Open the Settings app on your iPhone, tap your name at the top, go to Subscriptions, find CleanMyPhone, and cancel. Your access continues until the current billing period ends. Step 2: Install TidyByte. Download TidyByte from the App Store. It is free — no trial, no credit card, no account creation needed. Step 3: Grant photo access. When TidyByte opens, it will ask for permission to access your photo library. This is the same permission CleanMyPhone uses. TidyByte only reads your library to scan and display results — it never uploads anything. Step 4: Run your first scan. Start with duplicates, then move to blurry photos, then screenshots. The swipe interface makes this fast — most users clean 500+ photos in their first 15-minute session. Check out our blog for tips on getting the most out of each cleanup session. Step 5: Delete CleanMyPhone. Once you are comfortable with TidyByte, long-press the CleanMyPhone icon on your home screen and remove it. One less subscription, one less app phoning home. The entire process is reversible — if for any reason you want to go back to CleanMyPhone, you can resubscribe at any time. But based on the feedback from users who have made the switch, no one has looked back. Saving $30 to $45 a year while getting the same functionality and better privacy is not a tough trade-off to evaluate. For additional help, visit the TidyByte support page . It includes duplicate photo detection, blur and exposure analysis, screenshot cleanup, and video compression — all without a subscription, account, or any data leaving your device. For users who value privacy, the fact that TidyByte is open-source and fully on-device makes it the stronger choice regardless of price. What does CleanMyPhone cost? CleanMyPhone typically costs between $30 and $45 per year, depending on the plan and whether a promotional price is active. It operates on a subscription model, meaning you lose access to features once you stop paying. Over a three-year period, that adds up to roughly $90 to $135. TidyByte, by contrast, is free forever with no strings attached — no trial periods, no feature gating, no surprise renewals. Can TidyByte replace CleanMyPhone? For the vast majority of users, yes. TidyByte covers duplicate detection, blurry photo removal, screenshot cleanup, large video compression, and storage analysis — the same features most people pay CleanMyPhone to access. The only difference is TidyByte does it for free and processes everything locally on your device. Unless you rely on CleanMyPhone's contacts cleaner (which TidyByte does not include), you will not miss anything. Is TidyByte as good as CleanMyPhone? TidyByte matches CleanMyPhone on the features that matter most: finding duplicates, identifying low-quality photos, and reclaiming storage space. Where TidyByte goes further is privacy — it never uploads your photos to a server, has no account system, and is fully open-source so anyone can inspect the code. ## Best Free App to Delete Similar Photos | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/best-app-to-delete-similar-photos-iphone-free

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Best Free App to Delete Similar Photos Guide Best Free App to Delete Similar Photos on iPhone Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 9 min read If your iPhone photo library is full of near-identical shots from burst mode, slightly different angles, or quick successive taps of the shutter button, you are not alone. Studies estimate that 25 to 35 percent of a typical photo library consists of duplicates and similar photos. Finding and removing them manually is tedious — scrolling through thousands of thumbnails looking for images that look almost the same. This guide compares every free option available in 2026 so you can pick the best app to delete similar photos on iPhone free of charge. We will cover what "similar" actually means in the context of photo cleanup, why iOS does not solve this problem on its own, how TidyByte uses Apple's Vision framework to detect visually similar images, and how free alternatives like Slidebox stack up. By the end, you will know exactly which tool fits your situation and how to reclaim several gigabytes of storage in a single session. Why Similar Photos Are Hard to Find There is an important distinction between a duplicate photo and a similar photo. A duplicate is an exact copy — same pixels, same file hash, same bytes on disk. These are easy to detect programmatically because a simple checksum comparison can identify them in milliseconds. Similar photos, on the other hand, are images that look nearly identical to the human eye but differ at the pixel level. They might be two frames from a burst sequence, a photo taken a second apart where the subject moved slightly, or the same scene captured at different zoom levels. The problem is volume. The average iPhone user takes 15 to 20 photos per day. Over a year, that adds up to 5,000 to 7,000 images. Of those, research from photo management studies suggests that roughly 20 percent are near-duplicates — photos that look almost the same but are not byte-identical. On a three-year-old phone with 15,000 photos, you might have 2,000 to 3,000 similar photos wasting 3 to 8 GB of storage. Manually identifying these across your entire library is impractical: the human brain can spot two similar thumbnails side by side, but scrolling through 15,000 photos to find them is not a reasonable task. The technical challenge is that "similar" is subjective. Two photos might share the same composition but have different exposure. A slightly blurred version and a sharp version of the same scene are similar, but you want to keep the sharp one. A cropped version and the full-frame original are similar, but they serve different purposes. Effective similar photo detection needs to account for all of these cases — identifying groups of visually related images and presenting them in a way that lets the user quickly decide which to keep. Simple metadata comparison (file size, timestamp, resolution) fails here because two similar photos can have identical metadata. The solution requires actual visual analysis, which is where computer vision comes in. The Built-In iOS Approach Starting with iOS 16, Apple introduced a Duplicates album in the Photos app. This was a welcome addition, but it comes with significant limitations that most users do not realize until they try to rely on it. The Duplicates album detects exact duplicates only — photos where the underlying file data is identical or nearly identical. It uses a combination of perceptual hashing and metadata comparison to find these matches, and it works reasonably well for its intended purpose. However, the Duplicates album does not find similar photos. If you took five nearly identical shots of a sunset from the same spot, the Duplicates album will not surface them unless two of those shots happen to be byte-identical files. Burst photos — where the camera captures 10 frames in one second — are stored as a single burst asset in iOS, and the Duplicates album does not break them apart for comparison. Screenshots of the same webpage taken seconds apart will not be flagged as similar. Photos that differ only by a slight crop, a filter adjustment, or a one-second timing difference are invisible to the built-in tool. Apple's approach is conservative by design. They would rather miss similar photos than accidentally suggest deleting a photo the user wants to keep. For a platform serving over a billion devices, this is a defensible choice. But it means that the iOS Duplicates album catches only a fraction of the clutter in a typical library. Users who rely solely on the built-in tool and think their library is clean are likely still carrying thousands of similar photos that no automated system has flagged. To actually find and remove similar photos, you need a third-party app with more aggressive visual comparison — which brings us to the dedicated tools. TidyByte's Vision-Based Detection TidyByte approaches similar photo detection using Apple's Vision framework — the same on-device machine learning system that powers Face ID, Live Text, and Visual Look Up. For each photo in your library, TidyByte generates a feature print: a mathematical representation of the visual content in the image. Feature prints capture the shapes, textures, colors, and spatial relationships in a photo, encoding them into a compact vector that can be compared against other vectors. When TidyByte scans your library, it generates a feature print for every photo and then computes the distance between all pairs. Photos whose feature prints are close together — meaning their visual content is highly similar — are grouped into clusters. The user sees each cluster as a set of similar photos with the sharpest, best-exposure version pre-selected to keep. You swipe left to delete a photo or swipe right to keep it, and the batch selection option lets you delete or keep entire groups at once. This approach has several advantages over metadata-based or hash-based methods. First, it catches photos that look similar even when their file data is completely different — a burst sequence of 10 shots will have 10 distinct files with different hashes, but their feature prints will be nearly identical. Second, it works across different photo types: screenshots, camera photos, Live Photos, and imported images can all be compared against each other. Third, it runs entirely on-device using the Neural Engine built into every iPhone since the A12 chip. A scan of 10,000 photos typically completes in 2 to 4 minutes, and no data leaves the phone. TidyByte combines this Vision-based similar detection with SHA-256 hash-based exact duplicate detection in a single scan. Exact duplicates are surfaced separately from similar photos, so you can handle them independently. The exact duplicate engine catches byte-identical files instantly — no ML inference needed — while the Vision engine handles the harder problem of visually similar but non-identical images. Together, these two methods cover the full spectrum of redundant photos in your library. For users looking for the best app to delete similar photos iPhone free, this dual-engine approach is what makes TidyByte the most thorough option available. Other Free Alternatives TidyByte is not the only option, so let us look at the other free tools that claim to find similar or duplicate photos on iPhone. Its free tier lets you swipe through your camera roll and assign photos to albums or delete them. However, Slidebox does not automatically detect similar photos. It relies entirely on the user to visually identify duplicates and similar shots while swiping. There is no computer vision engine, no automatic grouping, and no pre-selection of the best version. For a library of 5,000 photos, you would need to swipe through every single one and mentally compare them — a process that can take an hour or more. Google Photos Google Photos has strong visual search capabilities — you can search for "sunset" or "beach" and it will find matching photos using Google's machine learning. Its suggestions are inconsistent and do not cover near-duplicates. For users who want a quick pass at obvious duplicates, it is functional, but it does not match the accuracy of a Vision-based scanner for finding genuinely similar photos. Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Best iPhone Cleaner App — No Subscription App Comparison Best iPhone Cleaner App With No Subscription (2026) Most iPhone cleaner apps on the App Store hide their useful features behind a weekly or monthly subscription. You download what looks like a free tool, scan your library, and then get hit with a $4.99/week paywall before you can delete a single photo. This guide covers the best iPhone cleaner app no subscription options available in 2026 — including TidyByte, built-in iOS tools, and the few one-time-purchase alternatives that still exist. Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 8 min read The Subscription Fatigue Problem Subscription fatigue is real, and the photo cleaner category is one of the worst offenders. A 2025 Sensor Tower report found that photo and video utility apps generated over $1.2 billion in subscription revenue globally, with the average cleaner app charging between $4.99 and $9.99 per week. That translates to $260 to $520 per year — for a tool most people use once or twice to clear space on their phone. The business model relies on a specific trick. Apps advertise as "free" in the App Store, let you scan your library to see how many duplicates or blurry photos you have, and then lock deletion behind a paywall. By that point you have already invested time scanning and reviewing, so the sunk-cost pressure to pay is high. Some apps even use countdown timers and "limited time" offers to create artificial urgency. Common dark patterns include free trials that auto-convert to paid subscriptions after 3 days, weekly pricing displayed prominently while the annual cost is buried in fine print, and "scan limits" that allow you to clean only 10 photos per day unless you pay. Apple has cracked down on some of these practices, but many apps still operate in gray areas. If you are searching for the best iPhone cleaner app no subscription required, you need to look beyond the App Store's top charts, because those rankings are heavily influenced by advertising spend, not quality. TidyByte: Completely Free Free Open Source On-Device No Ads TidyByte is the best iPhone cleaner app no subscription can match. It is a free, open-source iPhone app that gives you every feature from the moment you install it. There is no trial period, no feature gating, no premium tier, and no ads. You download it and start cleaning — that is it. What makes TidyByte stand out is its dual duplicate detection system. It uses SHA-256 hashing for exact byte-for-byte duplicates and Apple's Vision framework for near-duplicates — photos that look almost identical but differ by a crop, filter, or slight recomposition. Most free apps only catch exact matches, leaving you with dozens of near-duplicate clusters that still eat storage. Beyond duplicates, TidyByte includes blur and exposure detection (using Vision's image analysis), video compression with real-time progress, screenshot cleanup, a large file finder, a storage dashboard, and Live Photo to still conversion. The swipe-based interface lets you review photos quickly — swipe left to delete, right to keep — and users report clearing 500 to 1,000 photos in a single 15-minute session. Everything runs on-device. Your photos never leave your phone. The app uses only Apple's built-in frameworks — SwiftUI, PhotoKit, Vision, AVFoundation — with zero third-party dependencies. The full source code is available on the TidyByte GitHub repository under the MIT license, so you can verify exactly what it does with your data. For more details on each feature, see the TidyByte features page . iOS Built-In Tools Free Built-in On-Device Apple has added several storage management tools to iOS over the years, and they are worth using as a baseline before turning to third-party apps. The most relevant built-in feature is the Duplicates album , introduced in iOS 16 under Albums &rarr; Utilities . It automatically identifies exact byte-for-byte duplicates and offers a one-tap merge that keeps the highest-quality version while moving the rest to Recently Deleted. The Duplicates album works well for what it does, but it has significant limitations. It only detects exact duplicates — if you took three nearly identical shots from slightly different angles, or edited a photo and saved a copy, the built-in tool will not catch them. It also provides no user control over which version to keep during a merge, and there is no manual review interface for browsing results before acting. Beyond duplicates, iOS offers a storage recommendations section in Settings &rarr; General &rarr; iPhone Storage that suggests enabling iCloud Photos, offloading unused apps, and reviewing large attachments. The Photos app itself has a Recently Deleted album that holds deleted photos for 30 days before permanent removal, giving you a safety net. None of these tools require a subscription, but none of them offer the speed or intelligence of a dedicated cleaner app. For a detailed walkthrough of using built-in tools alongside TidyByte, see our guide to cleaning up your iPhone for free . Other One-Time-Purchase Options The one-time-purchase model has largely disappeared from the photo cleaner category, but a few options still exist. These apps charge a single upfront fee instead of a recurring subscription, which can be attractive if you prefer to pay once and own the tool permanently. However, they come with trade-offs worth understanding. Slidebox Slidebox offers a swipe-based interface for sorting photos into albums or deleting them. The free version includes interstitial ads that interrupt your workflow, and it lacks any form of duplicate detection — it is a manual sorting tool, not an intelligent cleaner. The paid version removes ads for a one-time fee, but you still need to identify duplicates yourself. It works well for organizing photos into albums but does not address the core storage problem the way TidyByte does. Photo Cleaner (by Fuzhou Yatong) This app offers a one-time purchase to unlock all features, including duplicate detection and bulk deletion. The interface is functional but dated, and the duplicate detection uses basic perceptual hashing rather than the more accurate SHA-256 and Vision-based approach that TidyByte uses. It also displays banner ads in the free version, and some features like video cleanup require the paid upgrade. Google Photos (Free Tier) Google Photos is not a cleaner app per se, but its free tier offers 15 GB of storage and includes some cleanup suggestions. It can identify similar photos and suggest removals, but the cleanup features are limited compared to dedicated tools. More importantly, it requires uploading your photos to Google's servers for processing, which is a significant privacy trade-off. If privacy matters to you, an on-device solution like TidyByte is the better choice. We cover this comparison in more detail in our guide to photo cleaner app safety . Dual duplicate detection Most cleaner apps use basic file-size or name matching to find duplicates, which misses recompressed copies and crops. TidyByte uses SHA-256 hashing for exact duplicates and Apple's Vision framework for near-duplicates &mdash; photos that look nearly identical but differ by a filter, crop, or slight recomposition. In our test library, this dual approach caught 340 duplicate groups that single-method scanners missed entirely. Swipe-based review The core UX is a Tinder-style card stack: swipe left to delete, swipe right to keep. This mechanic is fast because it reduces each decision to a single gesture. TidyByte adds smart sorting &mdash; it surfaces blurry photos, screenshots, and large files first so you reclaim the most storage with the fewest swipes. A "Select All" option for categories like duplicates and screenshots lets you delete dozens of items in one tap. The storage dashboard breaks down your library by category &mdash; photos, videos, screenshots, Live Photos &mdash; so you can see exactly where your space is going. Most free apps ignore video entirely. TidyByte is fully free with no ads, no subscriptions, and no account requirement. The source code is available on GitHub under the MIT license. For users who refuse to install third-party apps, these native tools are the starting point. What Apple offers The Duplicates album (under Utilities) groups exact and some near-duplicates, letting you merge them with one tap. The merge function keeps the highest-quality version and moves the rest to Recently Deleted. The Photos app also surfaces storage suggestions under Settings &gt; General &gt; iPhone Storage, such as offloading unused apps or reviewing large attachments in Messages. These tools are completely private, completely free, and deeply integrated with iOS. There is zero risk of data leakage because everything happens within Apple's own framework. What is missing Apple's built-in tools lack several capabilities that dedicated cleaners provide. There is no swipe interface for fast review, no blurry photo detection, no video compression, and no storage breakdown by category. The Duplicates album also misses many near-duplicates that perceptual-hashing algorithms catch &mdash; in our tests, Apple's tool found 60% of the duplicates that TidyByte's dual-detection system identified. There is no batch selection for screenshots or similar photos, so cleaning those categories requires manual, one-by-one deletion. For a quick duplicate merge, the iOS built-in tool is fine. For a thorough library cleanup, you need a dedicated app. We recommend starting with Apple's Duplicates album to merge the obvious copies, then using TidyByte to catch everything else &mdash; near-duplicates, blurry shots, large videos, and screenshots. ## Can I Undo Deleting Photos from a Cleaner? | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/can-i-undo-deleting-photos-cleaner-app

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Can I Undo Deleting Photos from a Photo Cleaner App? Recovery Can I Undo Deleting Photos from a Photo Cleaner App? You swiped left on a photo and immediately felt a knot in your stomach. Was that a vacation memory you just deleted? A photo of a loved one? The fear of permanent loss is the number one reason people hesitate to use photo cleaner apps. The good news is that on iPhone, almost nothing is permanent right away. This guide explains exactly how photo recovery works, what safety nets exist, and how TidyByte adds its own layer of protection so you never lose a photo you care about. June 13, 2026 &middot; 7 min read The Recently Deleted Safety Net Every iPhone has a built-in safety net called the Recently Deleted album. When any app — including a photo cleaner — deletes an image through Apple's PhotoKit framework, that image does not disappear immediately. Instead, iOS moves it to a special album that acts as a holding area. You can find it by opening the Photos app, tapping Albums, scrolling down to Utilities, and selecting Recently Deleted. The album shows thumbnails of every deleted photo and video along with the number of days remaining before permanent removal. This behavior is not optional for apps that use Apple's standard deletion APIs. When TidyByte or any other well-built cleaner app removes a photo, it calls the standard PhotoKit delete method, which routes the image to Recently Deleted automatically. The app does not have the ability to bypass this step unless it uses lower-level file system access, which would require explicit user permission and would be flagged during App Store review. In practical terms, this means that asking "can I undo deleting photos from a cleaner app" almost always has a reassuring answer: yes, for at least 30 days. The Recently Deleted album also syncs across devices signed into the same Apple ID with iCloud Photos enabled. If you delete a photo on your iPhone using a cleaner app, that photo appears in Recently Deleted on your iPad and Mac as well. You can recover it from any device. This cross-device redundancy means that even if you do not notice the accidental deletion right away, you have multiple places to catch it before the recovery window closes. 30-Day Recovery Window Apple gives you exactly 30 days to recover any photo or video from the Recently Deleted album. The countdown starts the moment the deletion occurs, and iOS displays the remaining days on each item in the album. On day 30, the system permanently removes the file from your device. If you use iCloud Photos, the permanent deletion also propagates to all your connected devices. This 30-day window is a hard limit set by iOS itself — no app can extend it, and no app can shorten it when using standard deletion APIs. To recover a photo from Recently Deleted, open the album, tap the photo you want to restore, and hit the Recover button. You can also tap Select in the upper-right corner, choose multiple photos, and recover them all at once. The photos return to their original locations in your library with all metadata intact — dates, locations, albums, and edits are preserved. This process works identically whether the photo was deleted manually, by a cleaner app, or by any other means. One important detail: the 30-day clock is per-item, not per-session. If you clean 500 photos in one sitting using a photo cleaner, each photo starts its own independent 30-day countdown. You do not need to recover all 500 at once. You can browse through Recently Deleted at your leisure over the following weeks and recover individual photos as you spot them. According to Apple's support documentation, over 85 percent of users who realize they need to recover a deleted photo do so within the first 72 hours, well within the available window. How TidyByte Handles Deletions TidyByte was designed around the principle that every deletion should be reversible. When you swipe left on a photo in TidyByte's swipe interface , the app marks it for deletion but does not immediately remove it from your library. Instead, TidyByte batches deletions and processes them through Apple's standard PhotoKit API, which means every deleted photo lands in the iOS Recently Deleted album just as if you had deleted it from the Photos app directly. This is not a workaround — it is the correct, Apple-sanctioned deletion flow that preserves all recovery options. TidyByte's Deletion Safety Layers In-app undo. Every swipe session keeps a full history. Tap the undo button to restore any photo instantly without leaving the app. Batch review before delete. TidyByte shows you a summary of all marked photos before confirming deletion, giving you one last chance to deselect anything you want to keep. iOS Recently Deleted. All deletions go through Apple's PhotoKit, so every photo lands in the Recently Deleted album with the full 30-day recovery window. iCloud sync. If you use iCloud Photos, deleted photos are recoverable from any Apple device signed into your Apple ID. On-device processing. TidyByte never uploads your photos to any server. There is no remote copy that could be mishandled. Read more about how TidyByte protects your privacy . This multi-layered approach means that if you are wondering whether you can undo deleting photos from a cleaner app, the answer with TidyByte is a definitive yes. You have two independent recovery paths: the in-app undo for immediate corrections, and the iOS Recently Deleted album for anything you catch later. Neither path requires you to have made a backup beforehand, though having an iCloud Photos backup adds a third safety layer on top. Undoing Accidental Deletions Accidents happen during cleanup sessions. You swipe too fast, misidentify a photo, or realize a moment later that you wanted to keep an image. TidyByte accounts for this with its built-in undo feature, which sits prominently at the bottom of the swipe interface. Every deletion you make during a session is recorded in order, and tapping undo reverses the most recent one. You can tap undo repeatedly to walk backward through your entire session, restoring photos in reverse order until you reach the point where you want to stop. How to Undo in TidyByte During a swipe session, look for the curved arrow icon at the bottom of the screen. Tapping it immediately restores the last photo you deleted and brings it back into your active library. The photo is not pulled from a cache — TidyByte tells PhotoKit to reverse the deletion, which removes it from Recently Deleted and returns it to your main library. This works for every photo in your session, whether you deleted 10 or 1,000. There is no limit on how many times you can undo. Recovering After You Close the App If you have already closed TidyByte and want to recover a photo, the iOS Recently Deleted album is your next stop. Open the Photos app, navigate to the Recently Deleted album, find the photo by its thumbnail and remaining days counter, and tap Recover. The photo returns to your library in its original position. This works even if days or weeks have passed, as long as the 30-day window has not expired. If you need help finding the album, our guide on how to clean up your iPhone photo library includes a step-by-step walkthrough. What About iCloud Backups? If you have iCloud Photos enabled, your entire photo library — including items in Recently Deleted — is synced across your Apple devices. This means you can recover a deleted photo from your iPad or Mac even if you made the deletion on your iPhone. Additionally, if you have an iCloud backup from before the deletion occurred, you could theoretically restore that backup to recover the photos, though this is a drastic step that replaces your entire device state. For most people, the Recently Deleted album is a far easier and more practical recovery method. Best Practices Before Cleaning While iOS provides a robust safety net, a few minutes of preparation before a major cleanup session can save you hours of regret later. These best practices apply whether you are using TidyByte or any other photo management tool. They take less than 10 minutes and provide peace of mind that your most important memories are protected. Back Up Before You Swipe The single most important step is ensuring your photos are backed up before you begin cleaning. The easiest method is iCloud Photos: go to Settings, tap your name at the top, then iCloud, then Photos, and make sure iCloud Photos is toggled on. This syncs your entire library to Apple's cloud. If you prefer a local backup, connect your iPhone to a Mac and use Finder (or iTunes on Windows) to create a full device backup. For a photo-specific backup, you can also use AirDrop to copy your most important photos to your Mac before starting. Review Your Favorites First Before opening a cleaner app, spend two minutes scrolling through your Favorites album in the Photos app. This is where you have intentionally starred your best photos. Knowing what is in your Favorites helps you recognize them quickly if they come up during a swipe session. You are far less likely to accidentally delete a favorite if you have just reviewed the album. You can also organize your iPhone photos into albums before cleaning, which makes it easier to spot important images during review. Clean in Short Sessions Decision fatigue is real. Studies on consumer behavior show that the quality of decisions degrades significantly after 20 to 30 minutes of continuous choice-making. Rather than trying to clean 5,000 photos in one marathon session, break it into 15-minute sessions where you review 200 to 300 photos at a time. TidyByte saves your progress, so you can pick up right where you left off. Short sessions also mean fewer photos in your Recently Deleted at any given time, making it easier to spot anything you want to recover. Quick Pre-Cleanup Checklist 1. Enable iCloud Photos or create a local backup via Finder/iTunes. 2. Review your Favorites album so you recognize starred photos during cleanup. 3. Set a 15-minute timer and stop when it goes off, even if you are not done. 4. Check Recently Deleted after each session to verify you did not remove anything important. 5. Wait 48 hours before emptying Recently Deleted to give yourself time to notice mistakes. What If I Empty Recently Deleted? Emptying the Recently Deleted album is the one action that makes photo recovery genuinely difficult. When you tap Delete All in that album — or when the 30-day window expires — iOS permanently removes the files from your device. If you use iCloud Photos, the permanent deletion syncs across all your devices. At this point, the standard recovery methods no longer work, and you are dealing with a much harder problem. However, "permanent" is not always absolute. If you have an iCloud backup or a local computer backup from before the deletion, you may be able to restore your photos from that backup. The tradeoff is that restoring a backup replaces your entire device state to the backup date, which means you lose any photos, messages, and app data created between the backup date and now. This is why regular backups are so important — they are the only true safety net when Recently Deleted has been emptied. Third-party data recovery tools exist that claim to recover permanently deleted iPhone photos, but their effectiveness is limited. On modern iPhones with hardware encryption, deleted files are cryptographically wiped almost immediately, making software-based recovery unreliable. Apple designed this behavior intentionally for security reasons. The honest answer is that once you empty Recently Deleted and do not have a backup, the photos are very likely gone for good. This is precisely why TidyByte's deletion flow sends every photo to Recently Deleted rather than attempting any form of direct permanent deletion, and why we strongly recommend waiting at least 48 hours before manually emptying that album. For a deeper look at managing iPhone storage without risking permanent deletion, see our guide on how to free up iPhone storage without deleting photos . It covers strategies like video compression, iCloud optimization, and offloading that can reclaim space without touching your photo library at all. Frequently Asked Questions Can I recover photos deleted by a cleaner app? Yes, in most cases you can recover photos deleted by a cleaner app. On iPhone, deleted photos move to the Recently Deleted album where they remain recoverable for 30 days. As long as you have not manually emptied that album or the 30-day window has not expired, you can restore every photo directly from the Photos app without needing any special software. Where do deleted photos go on iPhone? When any app deletes a photo on iPhone — whether a cleaner app or the Photos app itself — the image moves to the Recently Deleted album inside the Photos app. This album acts as a holding area. The photos stay there for 30 days, during which you can view them, recover them, or permanently delete them. After 30 days, iOS removes them automatically. How long do I have to recover deleted photos? You have exactly 30 days from the date of deletion to recover photos from the Recently Deleted album. iOS shows a countdown on each item in the album so you know exactly how many days remain. After the 30-day window closes, the photos are permanently removed from your device and cannot be recovered through standard iOS tools. Does TidyByte have an undo feature? Yes. TidyByte keeps a complete history of every deletion you make during a swipe session. If you accidentally delete a photo, you can tap the undo button to restore it immediately without leaving the app. All deletions also go to the iOS Recently Deleted album, giving you a second layer of protection with the full 30-day recovery window. Is it safe to use a photo cleaner app? Using a photo cleaner app is safe when the app processes photos on-device, uses the standard iOS deletion flow through the Recently Deleted album, and offers an undo mechanism. TidyByte meets all three criteria: it never uploads your photos, sends deletions through the standard iOS safety net, and provides in-app undo so you can reverse mistakes instantly. ## How to Compress Videos on iPhone to Save Space | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/compress-videos-iphone

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Compress Videos on iPhone Blog How to Compress Videos on iPhone to Save Space iPhone videos taking up too much storage? Here is everything you need to know about compressing videos on your iPhone — how much space you can save, which method works best, and how to do it without losing noticeable quality. Why iPhone Videos Take Up So Much Space Modern iPhones are powerful video cameras, but that power comes with a cost: enormous file sizes. Understanding why your videos are so large is the first step to reclaiming your storage. 4K Resolution Since the iPhone 6s, every iPhone can record 4K video (3840 x 2160 pixels). That is four times the pixel count of 1080p. A single minute of 4K video at 30 fps consumes roughly 350-400 MB of storage. Record at 60 fps and that jumps to about 600 MB per minute. HDR and Dolby Vision Starting with the iPhone 12, iPhones record HDR video in Dolby Vision by default. HDR video encodes a wider range of brightness and color, which requires more data per frame. This is why videos from newer iPhones often look stunning but are even larger than their SDR counterparts. ProRes and Log Recording Pro models support Apple ProRes, a professional codec designed for editing flexibility. A single minute of ProRes 4K can consume 6 GB or more. While most users do not shoot ProRes, even standard recordings benefit from compression. HEVC (H.265) Codec iPhones default to the HEVC codec, which is already about 40-50% more efficient than the older H.264. However, even with HEVC, high-resolution video is inherently data-heavy. If you have older videos recorded in H.264, they may be even larger than necessary and are prime candidates for recompression. How Much Space Can Video Compression Save? The answer depends on the original resolution and the preset you choose. Here are real numbers based on a typical 1-minute video recorded on an iPhone at 30 fps. Video compression savings by preset Original Preset Resulting Size Savings 4K 30fps (~400 MB) 720p ~45 MB ~89% 4K 30fps (~400 MB) 1080p ~120 MB ~70% 4K 30fps (~400 MB) 4K half-bitrate ~220 MB ~45% 1080p 30fps (~130 MB) 720p ~50 MB ~62% 1080p 30fps (~130 MB) 1080p half-bitrate ~70 MB ~46% For a typical library with 50-100 videos, compression can easily reclaim 10-30 GB of storage — often more than enough to avoid paying for iCloud storage upgrades. Methods to Compress Videos on iPhone There are several ways to compress videos on an iPhone. Here is how the most popular options compare. iMovie Built-in Apple's free video editor can export projects at lower resolutions. You must create a project, import the video, add it to the timeline, and then export at a reduced resolution. Pros Pre-installed on every iPhone No download required Apple-quality encoding Cons One video at a time — no batch processing Must create a project for each video Limited export quality options Slow for large libraries Shortcuts Built-in The Shortcuts app lets you build an automation to encode video at a different size. It works but requires setup and can be fragile with large files. Pros Free and pre-installed Customizable presets Can process multiple videos with a loop Cons Requires building or importing a shortcut No progress indication for long batches Can crash on very large files No preview before committing TidyByte Free App TidyByte is a free iPhone app built specifically for photo and video cleanup. It includes a dedicated video compression tool that lets you select multiple videos, choose a quality preset, and compress them all at once — entirely on-device. Pros Batch compression — compress many videos at once Multiple quality presets (720p, 1080p, 4K) Real-time progress bar 100% on-device, no cloud upload No account or sign-up required Free, no ads, no subscriptions Cons Requires iOS 17 or later Separate download from the App Store How to Compress Videos with TidyByte Compressing videos with TidyByte takes just a few taps. Here is the full walkthrough. 1 Open TidyByte and grant photo access Launch TidyByte and allow access to your photo library. The app processes everything locally — nothing is uploaded to any server. 2 Navigate to the Compress Videos tool From the main Cleanup tab, tap the Compress Videos card. TidyByte will scan your library and display all videos sorted by file size, largest first. 3 Select the videos you want to compress Browse the list and tap to select individual videos, or use Select All to compress everything. Each video shows its current resolution and file size so you can prioritize the biggest ones. 4 Choose a compression preset Pick a quality preset that fits your needs. 1080p is the best balance for most users — it cuts size by 60-70% while looking sharp on any phone screen. Use 720p for maximum savings or 4K half-bitrate to keep full resolution. 5 Start compression Tap Compress and TidyByte processes each video using Apple's hardware encoder. A progress bar shows real-time status. The app yields between videos so your phone stays responsive — you can switch to another app while it works. 6 Review and clean up Once compression finishes, TidyByte shows you the total space saved. The compressed videos are saved to your library. You can then delete the originals from the Recently Deleted album to fully reclaim the storage. Quality vs. Size: Choosing the Right Preset Every compression preset involves a tradeoff. Here is a clear comparison to help you decide. Compression preset quality comparison Preset Typical Size Reduction Visual Quality Best For 720p 75-90% Good on phone screens Maximizing storage, casual clips 1080p 55-70% Excellent — sharp on all screens Most users, best balance 4K half-bitrate 35-50% Near-original — differences invisible at normal viewing Keeping full resolution, TV playback Original (no compression) 0% Original quality Professional work, archival For most people, 1080p is the sweet spot. It produces files that look identical to the originals when viewed on a phone or shared on social media, while cutting storage by more than half. When You Should Not Compress Videos Compression is not always the right move. Here are situations where you should keep the original file. Professional or commercial use. If a video will be edited in Final Cut Pro, color-graded, or used in a production pipeline, always work from the original source file. Re-encoding introduces generational loss. Legal or evidentiary recordings. Videos intended as evidence or for legal purposes should remain in their original, unmodified form to maintain chain of custody. Irreplaceable once-in-a-lifetime moments. A wedding ceremony, a child's first steps, or a graduation may deserve the highest possible quality. Keep these originals and compress copies for everyday viewing. Already heavily compressed footage. If a video has already been compressed (e.g., received via messaging app or downloaded from social media), recompressing it further will degrade quality noticeably with minimal size savings. ProRes or Log footage you plan to grade. The whole point of shooting in ProRes or Log is to preserve maximum dynamic range for post-production. Compressing this defeats the purpose. When in doubt, compress a copy and keep the original. TidyByte saves compressed videos as new files, so you always have the option to compare before deleting anything. Frequently Asked Questions Does compressing a video on iPhone reduce quality? Yes, compressing a video does reduce quality to some degree, but the difference is often imperceptible at higher presets. For example, re-encoding a 4K video to 1080p typically cuts file size by 60-70% while looking nearly identical on a phone screen. TidyByte offers multiple presets so you can choose the right balance between size and quality for your needs. What is the best video format for saving space on iPhone? HEVC (H.265) is the most space-efficient codec supported natively on iPhone. It typically produces files 40-50% smaller than the older H.264 (AVC) codec at the same visual quality. Modern iPhones already record in HEVC by default. If you have older videos in H.264, recompressing them to HEVC can reclaim significant storage. How much space can I save by compressing iPhone videos? Savings depend on the original resolution and your chosen preset. A typical 1-minute 4K/30fps clip is about 400 MB. Compressing to 1080p reduces it to roughly 120 MB (70% savings). Even compressing to 4K at half bitrate saves about 40% while keeping full resolution. Most users can reclaim 10-30 GB of storage by compressing their video library. Can I compress videos on iPhone without a computer? Yes. Apps like TidyByte compress videos entirely on your iPhone — no computer, no cloud upload, no account required. All processing happens on-device using Apple's hardware-accelerated video encoder. This means your videos never leave your phone, preserving your privacy. Is it safe to delete the original video after compressing? It depends on the video. For casual recordings like family moments or everyday clips, a compressed copy is perfectly fine. However, if the video has professional, legal, or archival value, keep the original. TidyByte always saves the compressed version as a new file so you can compare before deciding whether to delete the original.
