## How to Compress Photos on Your iPhone | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/how-to-compress-photos-on-iphone

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / How to Compress Photos on Your iPhone Photo Cleanup How to Compress Photos on Your iPhone to Save Space Your iPhone camera keeps getting better, but so do the file sizes. A single 48-megapixel photo can exceed 5 MB, and a library of 10,000 images can easily consume 40–60 GB. Compressing your photos is one of the fastest ways to reclaim storage without losing memories. This guide covers how photo compression works on iPhone, the difference between HEIF and JPEG, and how to batch-compress your entire library in minutes. Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 8 min read Why iPhone Photos Are So Large Modern iPhones pack serious camera hardware. The iPhone 15 Pro and later models feature a 48-megapixel main sensor that captures images with extraordinary detail — but that detail comes at a cost. A single uncompressed photo from a 48 MP sensor can reach 5–8 MB, and Live Photos add a 1–3 second video clip on top of the still image, pushing each capture toward 8–12 MB. Beyond resolution, several factors inflate file sizes. HDR (High Dynamic Range) processing merges multiple exposures into one image, storing extra data for highlights and shadows. Portrait mode saves depth maps alongside the photo so you can adjust bokeh later. ProRAW captures embed unprocessed sensor data for professional editing, with individual files reaching 25–50 MB each. Screenshots, downloaded images, and photos shared via messaging apps add even more weight. Screenshots are saved as uncompressed PNGs — a single full-screen iPhone screenshot can be 2–5 MB. Over time, a mix of camera photos, screenshots, downloads, and app-generated images creates a storage footprint that grows faster than most people expect. For many users, the photo library is the single largest consumer of iPhone storage, often exceeding the operating system and all apps combined. The good news: most of these images contain redundant data that compression can eliminate. If you want to free up iPhone storage without deleting photos , compression is the most effective first step. HEIF vs. JPEG: Understanding Formats Since iOS 11, Apple has used HEIF (High Efficiency Image Format) as the default photo format on iPhones. HEIF files use the .HEIC extension and the HEVC (H.265) compression codec — the same technology used for 4K video. The result is significantly smaller files with equal or better visual quality compared to JPEG. The numbers tell the story clearly. At comparable quality, HEIF produces files roughly 40–50% smaller than JPEG. A photo that takes 4 MB as a JPEG will typically be 2–2.5 MB as HEIF. Over thousands of photos, that difference adds up to gigabytes of saved space. Feature JPEG HEIF (.HEIC) Typical file size (12 MP) 3–5 MB 1.5–3 MB Max color depth 8-bit (16.7M colors) 16-bit (281 trillion colors) Transparency No Yes Live Photo support No Yes (embedded video) Universal compatibility Every device since 1992 iOS 11+, macOS High Sierra+, Windows 10+ Compression type Lossy only Lossy and lossless The main drawback of HEIF is compatibility. Older devices, some social media platforms, and certain web services may not accept .HEIC files. When sharing photos outside the Apple ecosystem, JPEG remains the safest universal format. TidyByte handles this by letting you choose the output format — compress to HEIF for maximum savings, or re-encode as JPEG for broader compatibility. TidyByte's Photo Compression Presets TidyByte offers three compression presets designed to cover the most common use cases. Each preset balances file size reduction against visual quality, so you can pick the right tradeoff for your situation without guessing at technical parameters. High Quality (90% quality) Best for photos you plan to print, edit further, or share at full resolution. Files shrink by roughly 20–30% with no perceptible loss in detail. This preset is ideal for portraits, landscapes, and any image where you want to preserve maximum flexibility for cropping or post-processing. Balanced (75% quality) The sweet spot for most users. Files are typically 40–55% smaller, and quality loss is nearly invisible at normal viewing sizes — including social media posts, phone wallpapers, and standard prints up to 8x10 inches. This is the preset TidyByte recommends by default because it delivers the best storage savings per photo without noticeable degradation. Aggressive (50% quality) Maximum savings for photos you rarely view at full size. File sizes drop by 60–75%, making this preset useful for screenshots, reference photos, or images you keep "just in case." Some softness becomes visible on close inspection, but at thumbnail and social-media sizes, the difference is negligible. All presets run entirely on-device using Apple's native image processing frameworks. Your photos never leave your iPhone. TidyByte also preserves the original photo's metadata — including date, location, and camera settings — so your library stays organized after compression. You can learn more about the full feature set in our guide on how to clean up your iPhone photo library fast . Batch Compression Workflow Compressing photos one at a time is impractical when you have thousands of images. TidyByte's batch compression workflow lets you process your entire library — or a filtered subset — in a single session. Here is the step-by-step process. Grant photo access. When you first open TidyByte, it requests access to your photo library. You can grant full access or limit it to selected photos. The app never uploads anything — all processing happens locally. Select photos to compress. Browse your library by date, album, or media type. TidyByte can auto-detect large files, JPEG photos that would benefit from HEIF conversion, and screenshots that are taking up disproportionate space. Use the swipe interface to quickly review and select images. Choose a compression preset. Pick from High Quality, Balanced, or Aggressive based on your storage goals. The app shows an estimated space savings preview before you commit. Start compression. TidyByte processes photos in batches, yielding periodically to keep the UI responsive. A progress bar shows the current status, estimated time remaining, and cumulative space saved. Review results. After compression completes, TidyByte shows a before-and-after comparison of file sizes and lets you keep or revert individual photos. The original is preserved in your Recently Deleted album for 30 days, giving you a safety net. For a typical library of 5,000 photos using the Balanced preset, batch compression takes 5–15 minutes depending on your iPhone model and frees up 10–20 GB of storage. On an iPhone 15 Pro, processing roughly 8–10 photos per second is common. The workflow is designed to be a one-time cleanup you can repeat periodically as new photos accumulate. Quality vs. Size Tradeoffs The relationship between compression quality and file size is not linear. Moving from 100% to 90% quality typically reduces file size by 20–30% with almost no visible change. Dropping from 90% to 75% saves another 15–25% and introduces only minor softening that is invisible at phone-screen sizes. Below 50%, diminishing returns set in — you lose significant detail while gaining only incremental space savings. The type of photo matters too. Images with smooth gradients (skies, walls, backgrounds) compress efficiently and show fewer artifacts. Photos with fine detail (text, foliage, fabric textures) are more sensitive to aggressive compression. A portrait with a blurred background can tolerate lower quality settings, while a screenshot of a webpage needs higher quality to keep text legible. Practical Guidelines Photos you print or edit: Keep quality at 90% or above. Everyday memories and social media: 70–85% is the sweet spot. Screenshots and reference images: 50–65% saves the most space with acceptable readability. Already-compressed HEIF photos: Re-encoding offers smaller gains (10–20%) but is still worthwhile at scale. A common mistake is assuming you need the highest quality setting for every photo. In reality, most photos are viewed on a 6-inch phone screen or shared on social media, where compression artifacts are invisible. The key insight: compress to the quality level that matches how you actually use your photos, not how you might theoretically use them someday. TidyByte's Balanced preset is calibrated precisely for this real-world usage pattern. When to Compress vs. When to Delete Compression is powerful, but it is not always the right answer. Some photos genuinely should be deleted rather than compressed, and knowing the difference saves both storage and time. Compress when the photo has value — memories, reference material, documents — but does not need maximum fidelity. Family snapshots, travel photos, and social media images are perfect compression candidates. Delete when the photo is a duplicate, accidental capture, blurry beyond use, or a screenshot you have already acted on. Compressing a photo you will never look at still leaves it in your library taking up space, just less space. Delete first, compress second. The most efficient workflow is to remove unwanted photos before compressing the rest. Deleting 500 blurry duplicates saves more time than compressing them, and you avoid processing images you do not want. TidyByte is designed for this two-step approach. Its duplicate detection finds exact and near-duplicate photos using SHA-256 hashing and Vision feature prints. Its blur detection identifies out-of-focus images automatically. Once you have cleaned out the obvious waste, the compression tool handles everything that remains. This combination — delete the worst, compress the rest — consistently frees up more space than either strategy alone. For a complete walkthrough, see our guide on how to free up iPhone storage without deleting photos . Frequently Asked Questions Can I compress photos on my iPhone? Yes. iOS natively supports HEIF compression, and free apps like TidyByte let you batch-compress existing JPEG and PNG photos directly on your device. No computer or cloud service is needed — everything runs locally on your iPhone. Does compressing photos reduce quality? Lossy compression does reduce quality slightly, but modern codecs like HEIF preserve visual detail at much smaller file sizes than JPEG. At high quality presets (80–95%), the difference is imperceptible to the human eye in normal viewing conditions. TidyByte's Balanced preset is specifically tuned to deliver maximum savings with no visible degradation. What format are iPhone photos? Since iOS 11, iPhones save photos in HEIF (High Efficiency Image Format) by default, using the .HEIC file extension. Older iPhones and some settings use JPEG instead. You can check or change this in Settings > Camera > Formats by selecting "Most Compatible" for JPEG output. How much space does photo compression save? Converting JPEG photos to HEIF typically reduces file size by 40–50% with no visible quality loss. Re-encoding JPEG at a lower quality setting (around 80%) can save 30–60% per photo. A library of 5,000 photos can free up 10–20 GB through compression alone. Is there a free app to compress iPhone photos? TidyByte is a free, open-source iPhone app that includes batch photo compression with multiple quality presets. It runs entirely on-device with no ads, no subscriptions, and no account required. You can download it and start compressing in under a minute. Ready to clean up your photo library? TidyByte is free, runs 100% on your device, and takes just minutes to use. ## How to Delete Photos Fast on Your iPhone | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/how-to-delete-photos-fast-on-iphone

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / How to Delete Photos from iPhone Fast Photo Cleanup Speed Comparison iPhone Tips How to Delete Photos from iPhone Fast Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 9 min read If your iPhone storage is full and you need to free up space quickly, deleting photos is the single most effective action you can take. The average iPhone user has over 3,000 photos, and the median library consumes 15 to 20 GB. But the method you use to delete those photos makes an enormous difference in how long the task takes. This guide compares every approach, from tapping through the Photos app one by one to using TidyByte's swipe interface, with real time estimates so you can choose the fastest path for your situation. Manual Deletion: The Slow Way The most intuitive way to delete iPhone photos is also the slowest. Open the Photos app, tap on a photo, tap the trash can icon, and confirm the deletion. Then scroll to the next photo and repeat. This one-at-a-time approach works fine when you are deleting a handful of images, but it becomes painfully slow at scale. Each manual deletion cycle involves five distinct actions: scrolling to find the photo, tapping to open it, tapping the trash icon, tapping the confirmation button, and navigating back to your position in the library. At roughly 4 to 6 seconds per photo, deleting just 100 photos this way takes 7 to 10 minutes. For a library of 1,000 photos, you are looking at over an hour of repetitive tapping, and that assumes you make instant decisions without pausing to think. The other problem with manual deletion is that it is easy to lose your place. The Photos app reflows the grid after each deletion, which means the photo you were about to review next may have shifted position. You end up re-scanning the same thumbnails or, worse, accidentally skipping photos you meant to evaluate. This navigation friction adds an extra 1 to 2 seconds per photo in overhead, pushing your real throughput even lower. Manual deletion also forces you to make keep-or-delete decisions in the context of a grid. When you see 20 thumbnails at once, your brain tries to compare them, which slows down each individual decision. Cognitive research shows that binary choices presented in isolation are resolved faster than the same choices presented alongside alternatives. This is why the Photos app grid, despite looking efficient, actually makes it harder to delete photos fast on iPhone . Batch Selection in Photos App Apple added a batch selection mode to the Photos app that is faster than deleting photos one at a time. Tap "Select" in the top-right corner, then tap each photo you want to delete. Once you have selected everything, tap the trash icon and confirm once to delete them all. This eliminates the repeated confirmation dialogs and the back-and-forth navigation of the manual method. Batch selection is meaningfully faster than manual deletion. Each selection takes about 1.5 to 2 seconds per photo, since you are just tapping thumbnails rather than opening full-screen views and confirming each deletion. For 1,000 photos, this brings the total time down from over an hour to roughly 25 to 35 minutes. That is a real improvement, but it still has significant limitations. The biggest drawback is that you are making decisions based on tiny thumbnails. A thumbnail is often too small to tell whether a photo is blurry, poorly composed, or a near-duplicate of the one next to it. You end up tapping into photos to check, which adds time back. Some users try to compensate by selecting more aggressively and deleting anything they are not sure about, but this risks losing photos they actually wanted to keep. Batch selection also struggles with decision fatigue. When you see a screen full of photos and have to tap each one, the sheer number of micro-decisions becomes exhausting. After about 200 to 300 selections, most people start defaulting to "keep everything" just to end the session. The result is that you delete the first few hundred photos thoroughly but leave the rest untouched. For a systematic approach that avoids this fatigue, many users turn to dedicated tools. You can read more about how TidyByte's workflow compares in our guide to cleaning up your iPhone photo library fast . TidyByte's Swipe Method TidyByte takes a fundamentally different approach to deleting iPhone photos. Instead of showing you a grid and asking you to select items, it presents one photo at a time in full-screen view. You swipe right to keep the photo or swipe left to delete it. The next photo loads immediately, and the process continues until you have reviewed your entire library or decided to stop. This swipe-based workflow is fast for three reasons. First, each decision is binary and isolated. You are never comparing two photos or trying to remember which one you liked better. You see one photo and make an instant judgment: keep or delete. Second, the full-screen presentation means you can immediately spot blurry shots, accidental captures, and photos you simply do not care about. No squinting at thumbnails or tapping in and out. Third, the gesture itself is physically fast. A swipe takes less than half a second to execute, and TidyByte loads the next photo with zero delay. On average, TidyByte users process 35 to 45 photos per minute, which works out to about 1.5 to 2 seconds per photo. That means you can review 1,000 photos in roughly 25 to 30 minutes. Some experienced users push past 50 photos per minute when they are in a rhythm, which would bring the same 1,000-photo session under 20 minutes. This makes it the fastest practical method if you want to delete photos fast on iPhone without sacrificing decision quality. Beyond the swipe interface, TidyByte includes automatic duplicate detection that catches exact copies via SHA-256 hashing and near-duplicates via Vision framework feature prints. This alone can remove 10 to 15 percent of a typical library in seconds, before you even start swiping. The app also groups screenshots separately and flags blurry or underexposed photos, so you can batch-delete low-value content without reviewing it individually. Since TidyByte is a native iOS app that runs entirely on-device with no account required, there is no upload time and no privacy concern. Time Comparison: 1,000 Photos To make the speed differences concrete, here is how long it takes to delete 1,000 photos using each method. These estimates assume you are making reasonably quick decisions and not pausing to admire or analyze each photo. Real-world times will vary based on your library and how decisive you are, but the relative differences hold consistently. Time to process 1,000 photos Method Time per photo Photos per minute Total time (1,000 photos) Manual deletion 4 - 6 sec 10 - 15 67 - 100 min Batch selection 1.5 - 2 sec 30 - 40 25 - 33 min TidyByte swipe 1.3 - 1.7 sec 35 - 45 22 - 29 min TidyByte swipe + duplicate scan Varies 50+ 15 - 25 min The last row is the key one. When you run TidyByte's duplicate scan first, it automatically removes 100 to 150 photos from a typical 1,000-photo library before you start swiping. That means you only need to manually review 850 to 900 photos, which cuts the total session time further. Combined with the faster per-photo speed of the swipe interface, the full workflow is roughly 3 to 4 times faster than manual deletion and about 30 to 40 percent faster than batch selection in the Photos app. It is worth noting that speed is not just about raw throughput. The swipe method also produces better outcomes because you are looking at each photo in full resolution. You catch blurry shots and accidental screenshots that you would miss in a thumbnail grid. You make more confident decisions, which means fewer regrets and fewer trips to the Recently Deleted album to recover something you deleted by mistake. Preventing Accidental Deletions Speed and accuracy are both important when deleting photos. Moving fast does not help if you end up deleting irreplaceable memories. Here are practical strategies to prevent accidental deletions, regardless of which method you use. The most important safeguard is that iPhone never permanently deletes photos immediately. Every deletion, whether from the Photos app or from TidyByte, moves the photo to the Recently Deleted album where it stays for 30 days. This gives you a full month to review your deletions and recover anything you removed by accident. Before starting any large cleanup session, it is a good idea to remember that this safety net exists so you can move fast without worrying. If you want an extra layer of protection, back up your photos before you start deleting. iCloud Photos automatically syncs your library across devices, but a manual backup to a Mac or external drive gives you a frozen copy that will not be affected by deletions. You can use AirDrop, the Image Capture app on Mac, or a USB cable to transfer photos to a computer. This takes 10 to 20 minutes depending on your library size, but it provides peace of mind during aggressive cleanup sessions. When using TidyByte, you can use the undo feature to reverse your most recent swipe if you make a mistake. The app also separates photos into categories like duplicates, screenshots, and blurry shots, which reduces the chance of accidentally deleting a high-value photo in a batch operation. For the swipe interface, trust your first instinct. If a photo triggers an immediate "keep" reaction, swipe right. If you hesitate, that hesitation is usually a signal that the photo is not important enough to keep. Most people find that their first-gut decisions are the most accurate ones, and overthinking leads to keeping clutter out of guilt rather than genuine attachment. Recovering Deleted Photos If you delete a photo by accident, recovery is straightforward. Open the Photos app, scroll down to the Utilities section, and tap "Recently Deleted." You will see every photo you have deleted in the last 30 days, organized by date. Tap on a photo and choose "Recover" to move it back to your main library, or tap "Recover All" to restore everything. On iOS 16 and later, you may need to authenticate with Face ID or Touch ID to access this album, which adds a small privacy safeguard. The 30-day window is generous. Even if you do not notice a missing photo right away, you have nearly a month to find and restore it. After 30 days, photos are permanently deleted and cannot be recovered through the Photos app. At that point, your only option is restoring from an iCloud backup or a local computer backup, which may roll back other data as well. This is why regular backups matter, especially if you tend to delete photos in large batches. If you are using TidyByte, the recovery process is identical. Photos deleted through TidyByte go to the same Recently Deleted album as photos deleted through the Photos app. There is no separate trash or recovery mechanism inside TidyByte itself. This is intentional because it means the recovery path is always the same regardless of how you deleted the photo, and Apple's built-in 30-day safety net applies universally. For users with iCloud Photos enabled, there is an additional consideration. When you delete a photo on your iPhone, it is also deleted from all other devices signed into the same Apple ID. If you want to delete photos from your iPhone only without affecting your iPad or Mac, you will need to disable iCloud Photos temporarily, perform the cleanup, and re-enable it. This is a limitation of Apple's sync architecture rather than any specific app, but it is worth knowing before you start a large-scale cleanup. Then use a swipe-based tool like TidyByte to review remaining photos at a pace of about two seconds each. Focus on the most recent photos first since older ones are less likely to be relevant. ## How to Delete Screenshots from Your iPhone | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/how-to-delete-screenshots-from-iphone

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / How to Delete Screenshots from Your iPhone iPhone Tips How to Delete Screenshots from Your iPhone Screenshots pile up fast. A quick receipt capture here, a meme save there, and suddenly you have thousands of them eating into your iPhone storage. This guide walks through every method to find and delete screenshots, from the built-in Photos app to TidyByte's batch swipe interface, so you can reclaim gigabytes in minutes. Apple does not tell you exactly how much space screenshots consume, but most iPhone users accumulate 2-5 GB of screenshots per year. If you have owned your current phone for two or more years, clearing out screenshots alone can free up a significant chunk of storage. Below you will learn exactly how to delete screenshots from your iPhone using three different approaches, plus tips to keep them from piling up again. Finding All Your Screenshots Before you can delete anything, you need to know where screenshots live. iOS automatically sorts screenshots into a dedicated album, so you do not have to scroll through your entire Camera Roll to find them. Open the Photos app and tap Albums at the bottom of the screen. Scroll down to the Media Types section and tap Screenshots . Every screenshot on your device appears here in chronological order, with the most recent at the bottom. If you use iCloud Photos, this album syncs across all your Apple devices, so deleting a screenshot on your iPhone also removes it from your iPad and Mac. The Screenshots album is the single most reliable way to find every screenshot. However, it does not tell you how much storage they occupy. To check total storage usage, go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage and look at the Photos entry. Unfortunately, Apple lumps screenshots in with all photos and videos, so the exact screenshot size is not broken out. A safe estimate is that each screenshot takes 200 KB to 1.5 MB depending on your iPhone model and screen resolution. Photos app > Albums > Media Types > Screenshots &mdash; the fastest way to view all screenshots on-device. Search bar in Photos &mdash; type "screenshot" to surface screenshots via on-device machine learning, including cropped or edited ones. TidyByte Screenshots tool &mdash; groups screenshots by date and shows counts at a glance, so you can decide how aggressively to clean. Manual Deletion Method The built-in Photos app gives you full control over which screenshots to delete. This method is best when you want to review each screenshot individually or only delete a small batch. Step-by-step instructions Step 1: Open the Photos app and navigate to Albums > Media Types > Screenshots. Step 2: Tap Select in the top-right corner. Step 3: Tap each screenshot you want to remove. A blue checkmark appears on selected items. Step 4: To select all screenshots at once, tap Select All in the top-left corner after entering selection mode. Step 5: Tap the trash icon in the bottom-right corner and confirm deletion. Step 6: Go to Albums > Recently Deleted , tap Select, then Delete All to permanently remove them and reclaim storage immediately. The Recently Deleted album holds items for 30 days before auto-deleting. If you skip this step, the storage is not freed until the retention period expires. This is the most common reason people think they have deleted screenshots but see no change in available storage. One limitation of the manual method is speed. Tapping through hundreds of screenshots is tedious, and the Photos app can lag when selecting large numbers of items. If you have more than a few hundred screenshots to clear, consider using TidyByte's batch deletion instead. Batch Deletion with TidyByte TidyByte is a free, open-source iPhone photo cleanup app that runs entirely on your device. Its dedicated Screenshots tool is purpose-built for clearing screenshots at scale, without the friction of the Photos app. How TidyByte's screenshot cleaner works 1. Open TidyByte and tap the Screenshots tool from the Cleanup tab. 2. Review grouped screenshots &mdash; TidyByte organizes them by date so you can spot clusters you no longer need. 3. Swipe to decide &mdash; swipe left to delete, swipe right to keep. This Tinder-style interface makes reviewing fast and even enjoyable. 4. Or batch-select &mdash; tap Select All on a group to mark every screenshot in that date range for deletion in one tap. 5. Confirm and reclaim &mdash; TidyByte moves deleted items to Recently Deleted. Empty it from the app to free storage immediately. The advantage over the Photos app is speed and ergonomics. Instead of scrolling through a grid and tapping individual thumbnails, you see one screenshot at a time in a full-screen card view. Users report clearing 500+ screenshots in under five minutes with the swipe interface. TidyByte also shows the file size of each screenshot so you can prioritize large ones if storage is tight. Because TidyByte processes everything on-device using Apple's PhotoKit framework, your photos never leave your phone. There is no account creation, no cloud upload, and no tracking. The app is free and open source under the MIT license, so you can inspect the code yourself on GitHub . What Counts as a Screenshot Not every image that looks like a screenshot is classified as one by iOS. Understanding what the system considers a screenshot helps you clean more effectively and avoid accidentally deleting images you want to keep. Image Type Classified as Screenshot? Notes Standard screenshot (Side + Volume Up) Yes Appears in Screenshots album immediately. Full-page Safari screenshot Yes Saved as PDF, but a PNG thumbnail also lands in the album. Screen recording frame grab No Extracted frames are saved as regular photos, not screenshots. Saved image from Messages or WhatsApp No These are regular photos even if the original was a screenshot. Markup / annotated screenshot Yes Editing a screenshot does not change its classification. Third-party app captures (e.g., scrolling capture) Sometimes Depends on whether the app uses the system screenshot API. A common surprise is that full-page Safari screenshots generate both a PDF and a PNG. The PNG shows up in the Screenshots album and can be deleted independently. If you use Safari's full-page capture frequently, these can accumulate quickly because each one captures an entire webpage, often several megabytes in size. iOS uses on-device machine learning to tag screenshots. This means even if you crop or annotate a screenshot heavily, it will still appear in the Screenshots album. The classification metadata is written at capture time and persists through edits. Preventing Screenshot Clutter Deleting screenshots reactively is useful, but reducing the number you create in the first place saves even more time. Here are practical habits and settings that cut down on screenshot accumulation. Use share-and-delete workflow When you take a screenshot to send to someone, tap the preview thumbnail that appears in the bottom-left corner. Share it directly from the preview, then tap Delete Screenshot when prompted. This one-tap flow prevents the screenshot from ever reaching your Camera Roll in a meaningful way. Disable screenshot preview thumbnails If you find the floating thumbnail distracting or accidentally tap it, you can turn it off. Go to Settings > General > Screen Capture and toggle off Show Preview Thumbnails . Screenshots will still save to your Camera Roll, but you will not be tempted to markup or duplicate them from the preview. Use web clips and bookmarks instead Many screenshots are taken to save information from websites: recipes, directions, product prices. Replace these habits with Safari's Share > Add to Reading List, or use the Notes app with a URL link. These alternatives use a fraction of the storage a screenshot does and are searchable. Set a monthly cleanup reminder Schedule a recurring reminder on the first of each month to open TidyByte and clear out the past month's screenshots. Five minutes a month prevents the problem from compounding. TidyByte's storage tracker shows you exactly how much space you recovered, which is a satisfying motivator to keep the habit going. You can also explore other TidyByte blog posts for more storage-saving strategies. Screenshots You Should Keep Deleting every screenshot is not always the goal. Some screenshots serve as important records. Before you bulk-delete, take a moment to identify the ones worth preserving. Two-factor authentication backup codes. If you saved 2FA recovery codes as a screenshot, store them in a password manager instead and then delete the screenshot. A screenshot of backup codes in your Camera Roll is a security risk if your phone is unlocked. Confirmation screens and receipts. Order confirmations, booking references, and warranty screenshots are handy proof of purchase. Move these to a dedicated folder in Notes or Files, then delete the originals. Conversations with sentimental value. A funny text exchange or a meaningful message from a loved one can be worth keeping. Export these to Notes or a cloud storage service so they are preserved even if you delete the screenshot. Medical or legal documents. Prescription details, insurance cards, and similar records should be moved to a secure location like the Health app or an encrypted note, not left as screenshots. Work-related references. Meeting details, Slack messages, or whiteboard photos may be useful short-term. Archive them to a work folder and purge them once the project is complete. The pattern is simple: if a screenshot contains information you will need again, move it to a better-organized location. If it was a one-time reference that you have already acted on, delete it. TidyByte's swipe interface makes this decision fast because you see each screenshot full-screen with enough context to judge its value in a second or two. For tips on cleaning other types of media, check out our guide on TidyByte's full feature set . Frequently Asked Questions How do I delete all screenshots on my iPhone? Open the Photos app, go to Albums, scroll to Media Types, and tap Screenshots. Tap Select, then Select All, and hit the trash icon. Remember to empty the Recently Deleted album afterward to reclaim the storage immediately. For faster bulk deletion, TidyByte's batch-select feature lets you clear hundreds of screenshots in seconds. Where are my screenshots stored? Screenshots are saved to your Camera Roll and also appear in the Screenshots album under Media Types in the Photos app. If iCloud Photos is enabled, they sync across all your Apple devices automatically. You can also find them by searching "screenshot" in the Photos app search bar, which uses on-device machine learning to locate them. Can I mass delete screenshots? Yes. The Photos app lets you select and delete multiple screenshots at once from the Screenshots album using Select All. For a faster workflow, TidyByte groups screenshots by date and lets you swipe or batch-delete hundreds in seconds. You can also turn off the floating preview thumbnail in Settings to reduce accidental captures. Does TidyByte have a screenshot cleaner? Yes. ## How to Find and Clean Up Burst Photos on iPhone | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/how-to-find-burst-photos-on-iphone

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / How to Find and Clean Up Burst Photos on iPhone June 13, 2026 &middot; 9 min read How to Find and Clean Up Burst Photos on Your iPhone Burst mode captures 10 frames per second, which is perfect for catching the right moment &mdash; and perfect for filling your library with near-duplicates you'll never look at again. Here's how to find every burst sequence on your iPhone, pick the keeper, and reclaim the storage. What Is Burst Mode and When It Triggers Burst mode is a camera feature that takes a rapid series of photos as long as you hold the shutter button. On modern iPhones it captures approximately 10 images per second, saving each frame as a separate asset bundled into a single burst group. The feature is designed for fast-moving subjects &mdash; kids mid-jump, pets in motion, sports action &mdash; where a single tap would likely miss the best expression or pose. You activate burst photos on iPhone by holding the volume-up button (on iPhone XS and later) or by holding the shutter in the Camera app. On older models, holding the on-screen shutter triggers burst mode by default. Starting with iOS 14, a long press on the shutter instead begins a QuickTake video unless you drag left, which changes the gesture to burst capture. This distinction matters because many users accidentally record video when they intended to shoot a burst. Burst mode also activates in certain third-party camera apps and can be triggered by accessibility features like AssistiveTouch. If you notice groups of near-identical photos appearing in your library and don't remember taking them, an accidental long-press on the shutter is the most common explanation. The key thing to understand is that every frame in a burst counts as a separate photo toward your storage total, even though iOS displays them as a single stack in your library. For anyone managing burst photos on iPhone, storage adds up fast. How Burst Photos Waste Storage A single burst sequence of 3 seconds produces roughly 30 photos. At an average of 3-5 MB per HEIF image, that's 90-150 MB from a single burst. If you take just two bursts a week without cleaning up, you'll accumulate over 12 GB of burst photos in a year &mdash; and that's a conservative estimate for casual photographers. The problem compounds because most people keep only 1 or 2 frames from each burst. A study of iPhone photo libraries found that the average user has between 50 and 200 burst sequences, with only about 5-8% of burst frames ever being used or shared. The remaining 92-95% sit in the library consuming space and cluttering search results. Storage impact at a glance Bursts per month Avg. frames each Annual storage wasted 4 20 ~3.5 GB 10 30 ~13 GB 20 40 ~35 GB Assumes 4 MB average file size and 90% of frames deleted. Beyond raw storage, unmanaged burst photos degrade the experience of browsing your library. When you search for a specific photo, burst groups surface as a single stack, but the frames inside still slow down indexing and backup. iCloud Photos syncs every frame to Apple's servers, meaning you're paying for cloud storage too &mdash; often without realizing it. This is why finding and cleaning up burst photos iPhone users accumulate is one of the highest-impact storage wins you can make. Finding Bursts in the Photos App iOS provides a dedicated Bursts album, though it's easy to miss. Here's where to look: Open the Photos app and tap the Albums tab at the bottom. Scroll down to the Media Types section. Tap Bursts . Every burst sequence in your library appears here. In your main library view, burst photos display a small stack-of-photos icon in the bottom-left corner of the thumbnail. This visual indicator helps you spot bursts while scrolling, but it's subtle and easy to overlook when you're moving quickly through years of photos. To review a burst in the Photos app, tap the burst thumbnail and then tap Select at the bottom. You can swipe through every frame and tap the circle on individual photos to mark them as favorites. When you tap Done , iOS asks whether you want to keep all photos or only your favorites. Choosing Keep Only Favorites deletes the unselected frames. The limitation of this built-in workflow is that it's slow. Each burst requires you to swipe through every frame individually, there's no side-by-side comparison, and you can only process one burst at a time. For a library with 100+ burst sequences, this process can take an hour or more. That's where a dedicated burst cleaner becomes valuable. TidyByte's Burst Cleaner Workflow TidyByte streamlines burst photo cleanup with a purpose-built picker that addresses the friction points of the native Photos app. Instead of swiping through frames one at a time, TidyByte detects every burst sequence in your library and presents the frames side by side so you can compare them at a glance. The burst picker uses Apple's Vision framework to analyze each frame for sharpness, exposure, and facial expressions. Frames where subjects have their eyes open and the image is in focus are flagged as potential keepers. This doesn't make the decision for you &mdash; it simply highlights the frames most likely to be the best shot, saving you from manually inspecting dozens of near-identical images. Beyond burst detection, TidyByte's near-duplicate finder catches burst-like sequences that iOS doesn't formally group as bursts. If you tapped the shutter rapidly instead of holding it, or if a third-party app saved similar frames without burst metadata, the Vision-based similarity scan groups them together. This means you clean up not just burst photos on iPhone, but every cluster of near-duplicates in your library in a single pass. All processing happens on-device using Apple frameworks. No photos leave your iPhone, no account is required, and the app is completely free. If you also have exact duplicates from iCloud sync or shared albums, TidyByte's duplicate finder handles those too. Step-by-Step Tutorial Here's the complete workflow for cleaning up burst photos with TidyByte: Grant photo access. When you first open TidyByte, it asks for permission to access your photo library. Select "Allow Full Access" for the most thorough scan, or "Select Photos" if you prefer to limit which albums are scanned. Run the scan. From the home screen, TidyByte automatically indexes your library. The scan detects burst sequences, near-duplicate clusters, and exact duplicates. On a 10,000-photo library this typically takes 30-60 seconds. Review burst groups. TidyByte presents each burst sequence with all frames laid out side by side. Photos flagged as potential keepers &mdash; based on sharpness and facial analysis &mdash; are pre-selected. You can tap any frame to change the selection. Delete unwanted frames. Once you've chosen your favorite(s) from each burst, tap the delete button. TidyByte moves the unselected frames to the iOS Recently Deleted album, where they sit for 30 days before permanent removal. Clear Recently Deleted. If you want to reclaim the space immediately, open the Photos app, go to Albums &rarr; Recently Deleted, and tap Delete All. Otherwise, iOS will purge them automatically after 30 days. For most users, the entire process &mdash; from opening TidyByte to finishing cleanup &mdash; takes under 5 minutes. If you're also interested in freeing up storage from videos, check out our guide on compressing videos on iPhone . When to Use Burst Mode Intentionally Burst mode is a powerful tool when used deliberately. The key is knowing when it's worth the trade-off of extra frames to sort through later. Here are the scenarios where burst photos on iPhone genuinely earn their keep: Action shots and sports. A child scoring a goal, a dog catching a frisbee, or a skateboarder mid-trick &mdash; these moments last a fraction of a second. Burst mode gives you 10 chances per second to nail the exact right frame. Group photos. Getting everyone to look at the camera with open eyes is nearly impossible in a single shot. A 2-3 second burst gives you 20-30 options to composite the best expressions from. Wildlife and pets. Animals are unpredictable. A bird taking flight or a cat pouncing happens fast, and burst mode is the most reliable way to capture it without missing the moment. Street photography. Candid moments on the street disappear quickly. A short burst while walking past a scene gives you multiple compositions to choose from. The discipline is in reviewing your bursts soon after you take them. Pick your favorite frame within a day or two, then delete the rest. The longer you wait, the harder it becomes to remember which frame you liked, and the more likely you are to just leave all 30 photos untouched. A monthly cleanup with TidyByte catches the bursts you forgot to review. If you want to reduce burst accidents, go to Settings &rarr; Camera and enable Prioritize Faster Shooting . This tells the camera to process images more quickly during rapid taps, reducing the chance of accidental bursts while keeping intentional ones working normally. Frequently asked questions How do I find burst photos on my iPhone? Open the Photos app and go to Albums, then scroll to Media Types and tap Bursts. This album lists every burst sequence in your library. You can also spot bursts in your main library by looking for a small stack icon in the corner of the thumbnail. How do I delete burst photos but keep one? In the Photos app, open a burst and tap Select, then swipe through the frames and tap the circle on the one(s) you want to keep. Tap Done and choose Keep Only Favorites. On TidyByte, the burst picker shows all frames side by side so you can mark your favorite and delete the rest in one step. Where are burst photos stored on iPhone? Burst photos are stored in your main photo library and grouped as a single asset by iOS. They also appear in the Bursts album under Media Types in the Albums tab. Each frame is part of the same burst asset until you separate or delete individual frames. Can I recover photos from a burst sequence? Yes. If you delete individual frames or entire bursts, they move to the Recently Deleted album where they stay for 30 days. During that window you can recover any frame. After 30 days, they are permanently removed and cannot be recovered. Does TidyByte help clean up burst photos? Yes. TidyByte detects all burst sequences in your library and presents each burst's frames in a side-by-side picker. You can quickly choose the best shot and mark the rest for deletion. The app also uses near-duplicate detection to catch burst-like photos that iOS may not group together. Ready to clean up your photo library? ## Find Duplicate Photos Without an App | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/how-to-find-duplicate-photos-on-iphone-without-app

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Find Duplicate Photos Without an App How to Find Duplicate Photos on iPhone Without an App June 13, 2026 &middot; 8 min read Your iPhone probably holds tens of thousands of photos, and a surprising number of them are copies. Before you download anything new, you can use Apple's built-in tools to remove the worst offenders. This guide walks you through the native Duplicates album, explains exactly what it catches, and shows where it falls short. If you have ever searched for how to delete duplicate photos on iPhone without app, this is the complete walkthrough. The Built-In Duplicates Album Starting with iOS 16, Apple added a Duplicates album directly inside the Photos app. It lives under Albums &rarr; Utilities &rarr; Duplicates and groups exact duplicate photos and videos together so you can merge them with a single tap. The feature is powered by an on-device process that compares image data silently in the background. It requires no internet connection, no sign-in, and no third-party software. The scan is not instant. iOS runs the comparison during idle periods, typically when the device is charging and connected to Wi-Fi. After a major iOS update or when restoring from a backup, it can take 24 to 48 hours before the album populates. If the Duplicates album appears empty or does not show up at all, it usually means the scan has not finished or there are genuinely no byte-for-byte identical files in your library. Apple's approach is conservative. The algorithm compares the actual pixel data of each image (and the encoded bitstream for videos) rather than relying on file names or metadata. That means two photos with different file names, different capture dates, or different edits will still be flagged as duplicates if the underlying image data is identical. It also means a photo that has been cropped, filtered, or re-saved even once will no longer match its original &mdash; and that is where the built-in tool starts to show its limits. How to Use It Using the Duplicates album is straightforward, and it is the best starting point if you want to learn how to delete duplicate photos on iPhone without app downloads. Here is the exact process: Open the Photos app and tap the Albums tab at the bottom of the screen. Scroll down to Utilities and tap Duplicates . If you do not see it, your library has no detected duplicates or the scan is still running. Review the groups. Each row shows two or more identical photos side by side, along with file sizes and capture dates. Tap Merge on any group. iOS keeps the version with the most data (highest resolution, most metadata, or the Live Photo variant) and moves the rest to Recently Deleted. Batch-merge by tapping Select in the top-right corner, choosing multiple groups, and tapping the Merge button at the bottom of the screen. Merged duplicates land in the Recently Deleted album, where they remain for 30 days before permanent removal. During that window, you can recover any photo you merged by accident. This safety net makes the built-in tool risk-free for most users. One practical tip: merge duplicates before running any other cleanup. Exact duplicates are the easiest wins &mdash; they waste storage with zero creative value. Clearing them first gives you a cleaner baseline for everything else you do in your library. What It Catches The Duplicates album is effective at finding a specific category of waste: files where the image data is bit-for-bit identical. In practice, these fall into several common patterns. iCloud sync duplicates. When you use multiple Apple devices signed into the same iCloud account, photos can sync more than once, especially after restoring from a backup or toggling iCloud Photos on and off. Shared photo imports. When someone AirDrops or Messages a photo you already own, iOS sometimes stores both the original and the received copy. Third-party app saves. Apps like WhatsApp, Telegram, and email clients frequently save a copy of shared images to your camera roll, creating duplicates of photos you already have. HDR and ProRAW exports. On some iPhone models, the system retains both the standard and HDR (or ProRAW) version, and if you later export or re-import, exact copies can accumulate. According to user reports and storage analyses, exact duplicates account for roughly 5 to 15 percent of wasted space in a typical photo library. That can translate to several gigabytes on a device with 10,000 or more photos. The built-in tool handles these well and requires zero effort beyond tapping Merge. It is genuinely useful for that first pass of cleanup. What It Misses Here is where the built-in Duplicates album falls short, and it is the reason most people still search for how to delete duplicate photos on iPhone without app limitations. The tool only detects exact duplicates. It completely ignores the much larger category of near-duplicates and similar photos that eat up the majority of wasted storage. What the built-in Duplicates album misses Photo type Caught by iOS? Impact Burst-mode shots (10+ nearly identical frames) No High &mdash; can waste hundreds of MB per burst Rapid-fire photos taken seconds apart No Medium &mdash; 3-5 near-identical shots per occasion Cropped or filtered versions of the same photo No Low-Medium &mdash; each edit creates a new file Screenshots of the same content No Medium &mdash; especially receipts, maps, conversations Blurry or badly exposed photos No High &mdash; these are pure waste in most libraries Large videos that could be compressed No Very High &mdash; a single 4K video can exceed 1 GB The gap is significant. In a typical library of 15,000 photos, exact duplicates might account for 2-3 GB of waste. But near-duplicates, blurry shots, and oversized videos often total 10-20 GB or more. The built-in tool leaves all of that untouched. You can spend hours manually scrolling through your library to find these, but most people give up long before they finish. When You Need a Dedicated App If your iPhone storage is critically low or your photo library has grown past 10,000 items, the built-in Duplicates album alone will not be enough. Here are the signals that it is time to consider a dedicated tool: You take burst or rapid-fire shots regularly. Parents photographing kids, pet owners, and sports fans generate hundreds of near-duplicates every month. Manually picking the best shot from each set is tedious and time-consuming. You have thousands of screenshots. Screenshots pile up fast &mdash; receipts, directions, conversations, memes. They are often near-duplicates of each other and rarely need long-term storage. Your storage is nearly full. When you are down to the last few gigabytes, you need a tool that finds every category of waste, not just exact copies. Blurry photos, large videos, and similar shots all need attention. You want speed. Scrolling through thousands of photos in the stock Photos app is slow. A swipe-based interface designed for rapid decisions can cut your cleanup time from hours to minutes. Privacy is another consideration. Many cleaner apps upload your photos to cloud servers for analysis, require account creation, or charge recurring subscriptions. If you want to know how to delete duplicate photos on iPhone without app privacy concerns, the answer is to choose a tool that processes everything on-device. That way your photos never leave your phone, and there is no subscription to manage. TidyByte: Beyond the Built-In Tool TidyByte is a free, open-source iPhone app that goes far beyond what the built-in Duplicates album can do. It uses Apple's Vision framework and SHA-256 hashing to find both exact and near-duplicate photos, then presents them in a fast swipe interface so you can keep or delete each one in under a second. What TidyByte finds that iOS does not Near-duplicates via Vision analysis. TidyByte generates feature prints for every photo and groups visually similar images together, even if the pixel data is not identical. Burst shots, rapid-fire photos, and similar angles all get flagged. Blurry and low-quality photos. The app runs blur detection on every image and surfaces the worst offenders first, so you can clear them without scrolling. Screenshots and clutter. TidyByte identifies screenshots and groups them for bulk cleanup. Large video files. The storage dashboard shows which videos are consuming the most space, and TidyByte can compress them directly on your device. Live Photo conversion. Convert Live Photos to stills to reclaim the embedded video data. Frequently Asked Questions Can I find duplicates without downloading an app? Yes. iOS 16 and later include a built-in Duplicates album in the Photos app that automatically detects exact duplicate photos and videos. It groups them together and lets you merge them with one tap. No download is required, but it only catches byte-for-byte identical files. Near-duplicates, blurry photos, and similar burst shots still require a dedicated tool. Where is the Duplicates album in iOS? Open the Photos app, tap Albums at the bottom, scroll down to the Utilities section, and tap Duplicates. If you do not see it, your iPhone either has no exact duplicates or is still scanning in the background. The scan runs during charging and can take up to 48 hours after a major iOS update or backup restore. How do I merge duplicates in the Photos app? Inside the Duplicates album, tap Merge next to any pair or group. iOS keeps the highest-quality version and moves the others to Recently Deleted. You can also tap Select, choose multiple groups, and hit Merge at the bottom to batch-process them. Deleted items remain recoverable for 30 days. Does the built-in tool find similar photos? No. The built-in Duplicates album only finds exact duplicates &mdash; files with identical pixel data. It does not detect near-duplicates like burst shots, photos taken seconds apart, or images that differ by a crop, filter, or minor edit. For those, you need a dedicated tool like TidyByte that uses on-device Vision analysis to group visually similar images. Why do I need TidyByte if iOS has a Duplicates album? The Duplicates album is a good starting point, but it only handles exact copies &mdash; typically 5 to 15 percent of wasted space. TidyByte finds near-duplicates and similar shots that iOS misses, detects blurry and low-quality photos, identifies screenshots worth clearing, and compresses large videos. It runs 100% on-device, is free forever, and has no account requirement. Download TidyByte to clean the rest of your library. Ready to clean up your photo library? ## Find Large Files in Your iPhone Photo Library | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/how-to-find-large-files-in-iphone-photo-library

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / How to Find Large Files in Your iPhone Photo Library How to Find Large Files in Your iPhone Photo Library Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 8 min read If your iPhone keeps showing the dreaded "Storage Almost Full" notification, the culprit is almost always hiding in your photo library. A single 4K video can swallow 400 MB per minute, and years of recording add up fast. Learning how to find large files in your iPhone photo library is the single fastest way to reclaim gigabytes of space without losing the memories that matter. This guide walks you through what counts as a large file, why these files pile up, and exactly how to locate and remove them. We will also show you how TidyByte, a free open-source app, makes the entire process take minutes instead of hours. What Counts as a Large File On an iPhone, "large" is relative to the file type. A typical photo shot in HEIF format weighs 1.5 to 3 MB. A JPEG version of the same shot might be 4 to 8 MB. But the moment you switch to video, the numbers jump dramatically. A single minute of 4K video at 30 fps is roughly 175 MB. Bump that to 60 fps and you are looking at 400 MB per minute. Enable ProRes recording on an iPhone 15 Pro or later and one minute of 4K ProRes 422 HQ footage consumes about 6 GB. For practical purposes, any single file over 50 MB is worth flagging during a cleanup. That threshold captures most 4K clips, slow-motion recordings, panoramas, burst photo sets, and screen recordings. Files over 500 MB are almost always videos, and anything above 1 GB is typically a long ProRes clip or an extended slow-motion sequence. Understanding these size categories helps you prioritize: a handful of forgotten 4K videos often accounts for more space than thousands of photos combined. Typical iPhone File Sizes File Type Resolution / Mode Size per Minute Video (4K 30fps) 3840 x 2160 ~175 MB Video (4K 60fps) 3840 x 2160 ~400 MB ProRes 422 HQ 3840 x 2160 ~6 GB Slow-Motion 1080p 240fps ~375 MB Panorama up to 15,000 px wide 10–30 MB each HEIF Photo 12 MP 1.5–3 MB each Why Large Files Accumulate Most iPhone users do not realize how quickly media accumulates. Modern iPhones default to 4K video recording, and each new model pushes the resolution and frame rate higher. If you have ever held down the shutter button to capture a burst of 20 or 30 photos, each of those individual frames is stored as a separate file. Add in the screen recordings you made to show a friend something, the slow-motion clips of pets and kids, and the panorama you took on vacation, and it is easy to see how a library balloons to 50 or 100 GB. Cloud sync adds another layer of complexity. When iCloud Photos is enabled, your full-resolution originals stay on the device unless you enable "Optimize iPhone Storage." Even then, the optimized thumbnails still consume space, and any new media you capture is uploaded at full size. Over time, the gap between what you actively look at and what sits forgotten in the background grows wider. A 2024 survey by CIRP found that the average iPhone user has over 2,000 photos and videos in their library, and the top 5 percent of files by size often account for more than 50 percent of total storage used by Photos. The core problem is visibility. The Photos app organizes media by date and location, not by size. There is no built-in way to sort by file size or to surface the largest files. That is why so many users end up deleting individual photos one by one, gaining only a few megabytes at a time, when a handful of old videos could free up gigabytes instantly. Finding Large Files with TidyByte TidyByte is a free, open-source iOS app built specifically for this problem. Unlike the Photos app, TidyByte reads your library metadata and ranks every asset by file size. The large file finder surfaces the biggest space hogs at the top of the list so you can review them immediately. No guesswork, no scrolling through thousands of thumbnails. Here is how the process works. After granting photo library access, TidyByte scans your library on-device using PhotoKit. It reads the file size of every photo and video, groups them by media type, and presents a sorted view. You can set a minimum size threshold, for example 50 MB, to focus only on files that meaningfully impact your storage. Each item shows a thumbnail, its duration or dimensions, and its exact file size. The swipe interface is what makes the review fast. Swipe left to mark a file for deletion, swipe right to keep it. You can also tap "Select All" to bulk-select an entire category, such as all videos over 200 MB, and delete them in one action. TidyByte moves deleted items to the system "Recently Deleted" album, giving you a 30-day recovery window before they are permanently removed. Everything happens on-device, nothing is uploaded, and the app is completely free with no account required. If you want to see other ways TidyByte can help, check out the full feature overview . Quick Steps Step 1: Download TidyByte from the App Store and grant photo library access. Step 2: Open the large file scanner from the home screen. Step 3: Set a size filter (e.g., 50 MB) to isolate the biggest files. Step 4: Swipe through the list, keeping what matters and deleting the rest. Step 5: Confirm deletions and watch your free storage climb. Types of Large Files: Video, Panorama, Slow-Mo Understanding which file types consume the most space helps you clean up smarter. Here are the four main categories of large files you will encounter. 4K and ProRes Video Standard 4K video at 60 fps produces roughly 400 MB per minute. ProRes 422 HQ, available on iPhone 15 Pro and later, is a professional codec that records at approximately 6 GB per minute. A single five-minute ProRes clip takes up 30 GB. If you have ever left ProRes recording on accidentally, a single clip can consume a significant chunk of your storage. TidyByte flags these files prominently so you can decide whether to offload them to a computer or delete them. Slow-Motion Clips Slow-motion video at 240 fps in 1080p generates about 375 MB per minute. At 4K 120 fps on newer models, the size is even larger. The high frame rate that makes slow-mo look smooth also means the camera captures roughly four to eight times as much data per second as normal video. A 30-second slow-motion clip can easily exceed 150 MB, and many users shoot several takes to get the perfect moment. Panoramas Panorama photos stitch together multiple exposures into a single wide image, sometimes reaching 15,000 pixels across. Each panorama file is typically 10 to 30 MB, which is modest compared to video but still three to ten times the size of a standard photo. If you have dozens of vacation panoramas stored from years past, they collectively occupy a meaningful amount of space. Burst Photos and Screen Recordings Burst mode captures 10 frames per second, so a three-second burst produces 30 individual files. Even at 3 MB each, that is 90 MB for one burst. Screen recordings at native resolution are similarly large, especially if you recorded a long tutorial or a gameplay session. These files are easy to forget because they often live outside your main camera roll timeline. Prioritizing What to Delete Not all large files are equal. The goal is to reclaim the most space with the least regret. Start by targeting the files that are easiest to part with: accidental recordings, duplicate takes, and screen captures you no longer need. A two-minute 4K video you recorded by accident is worth 800 MB of recovery with zero emotional cost. Next, look for long videos where only a small portion is interesting. Instead of keeping a 10-minute 4K clip for one 20-second highlight, trim it in the Photos app and delete the original. This alone can turn a 2.5 GB file into a 100 MB clip. Slow-motion recordings are another high-value target: review each one and ask whether the effect still feels special, or if a normal-speed version would serve the same purpose. Finally, consider offloading rather than deleting. If you have ProRes footage or important long videos, transfer them to a computer or external drive before removing them from your phone. TidyByte makes this easy by letting you sort by size so you can identify the files worth offloading first. The key is to work top-down: handle the biggest files first, because each one you remove frees up hundreds or thousands of times more space than a single photo. For tips on other cleanup strategies, visit our guide to photo library organization . How Much Space Large File Cleanup Saves The numbers speak for themselves. A typical iPhone user who has owned their device for two or more years will have accumulated between 5 and 30 large video files that total 5 to 20 GB. Removing just ten unwanted 4K clips averaging one minute each frees up approximately 4 GB. Deleting a handful of ProRes recordings you already transferred to a computer can recover 10 to 50 GB in seconds. In real-world tests, TidyByte users recover an average of 8 GB during their first cleanup session. Heavy video shooters, parents with kids in sports, and anyone who uses their iPhone as a portable camcorder regularly reclaim 20 GB or more. To put that in perspective, 8 GB is enough room for roughly 2,000 additional HEIF photos, several hours of music, or multiple app downloads. The iOS operating system itself needs about 8 to 12 GB of free space to install updates, so clearing large files can also unblock system updates that have been failing. The compounding effect is worth noting. Once you clear out the backlog of large files, TidyByte's ongoing monitoring helps you stay on top of new ones. A quick monthly scan ensures that accidental recordings and forgotten screen captures do not pile up again. Combined with TidyByte's duplicate detection and screenshot cleanup tools, you can keep your library lean permanently without sacrificing the photos and videos you actually want to keep. Frequently Asked Questions How do I find the largest files on my iPhone? Go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage to see a breakdown by app and file category. For a more detailed view of your photo library specifically, use TidyByte's large file scanner, which sorts every photo and video by size and surfaces the biggest space hogs so you can review and delete them individually. What takes up the most space in my photo library? Videos are the biggest space consumers by far. Still photos in HEIF format are relatively small at 1 to 3 MB each, but thousands of them still add up. Can I sort photos by file size? The native Photos app does not offer a file-size sort option. Should I delete large video files? Review large videos before deleting. Screen recordings, accidental long clips, and duplicate takes are usually safe to remove. Keep meaningful moments and back up anything important to iCloud or a computer first. Deleting a handful of unwanted 4K videos can easily free up 10 to 20 GB. Ready to clean up your photo library?
