## iPhone Storage Full But No Photos? Here's Why | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/iphone-storage-full-but-no-photos

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / iPhone Storage Full But No Photos Storage Tips iPhone Storage Full But I Have No Photos? Here's Why Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 8 min read You deleted every photo, cleared your Camera Roll, and yet your iPhone still insists storage is almost full. If the "iPhone storage full but I have no photos" message has you staring at your screen in frustration, you are not alone. Apple's storage breakdown can be opaque, hiding gigabytes of data behind vague labels like "System Data" and "Other." This guide explains exactly where that missing space goes and gives you a concrete plan to get it back. Understanding 'Other' Storage Open Settings, tap General, then iPhone Storage, and you will see a color-coded bar at the top. One of those colors is labeled "Other" (or "System Data" on iOS 16+). This category is a catch-all for data iOS cannot neatly classify: system caches, downloaded Siri voices, Spotlight indexes, Keychain data, font files, and logs. On a healthy iPhone, Other storage typically sits between 5 and 15 GB. However, it can easily balloon past 25 GB when caches accumulate over months of use without a restart. The frustrating part is that Apple gives you almost no visibility into what lives inside Other. There is no "clear Other storage" button. Temporary files from streaming apps, failed iOS updates, and orphaned app data all pile up here. Safari alone can hold several gigabytes of cached web content. If you have ever watched a long video in a third-party app without closing it properly, the cached chunks may linger in Other for weeks. Restarting your iPhone once a week is the single most effective habit for keeping this category in check, as iOS purges many temporary files during the boot sequence. System Files and iOS Updates iOS itself requires a significant footprint. A fresh install of iOS 17 or iOS 18 occupies roughly 8 to 12 GB depending on your device model. That baseline is non-negotiable — you cannot shrink the operating system below its minimum. But the real space hog is a partially downloaded iOS update. When your iPhone downloads an update over Wi-Fi and you postpone installation, that 3 to 6 GB update file sits in System Data until you either install it or manually delete it. To remove a pending update, go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage, scroll to find the iOS update entry, tap it, and select "Delete Update." This alone can free up several gigabytes instantly. Beyond updates, system fonts, language packs for keyboards you no longer use, and diagnostic data all contribute. If you have enabled Share iPhone Analytics, diagnostic logs accumulate over time. You can disable this under Settings > Privacy &amp; Security > Analytics &amp; Improvements to prevent future log growth, though existing logs require a restart to clear. App Caches and Temporary Files This is where most people are genuinely surprised. An app's "App Size" in iPhone Storage might be 80 MB, but its "Documents &amp; Data" column can read 2 GB or more. Streaming apps like Spotify, Netflix, and YouTube are the worst offenders because they cache audio and video for offline playback and buffering. Social media apps — Instagram, TikTok, Snapchat — store hundreds of megabytes of viewed content, stories, and lens data. Even messaging apps accumulate cache from inline image previews and sticker packs. The key insight is that "deleting" an app from your home screen does not always clear its data if you chose "Remove from Home Screen" instead of "Delete App." To fully reclaim space, go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage, tap the app, and select "Delete App." Then reinstall it from the App Store if you still need it. Your account data is stored in the cloud, so you will not lose anything important. For apps you want to keep, look for an in-app "Clear Cache" option — many apps bury this in their settings menu. Doing this for your five largest apps can easily recover 5 to 10 GB. Messages and Attachment Storage iMessage is one of the most overlooked storage consumers. Every photo, video, voice memo, and document someone sends you in a conversation is stored locally by default. If you have been using iMessage for years without cleaning it up, your Messages app alone could be consuming 10 to 30 GB. Videos are particularly expensive — a single 60-second 4K clip shared in a group chat can exceed 400 MB. Apple introduced a helpful feature in recent iOS versions: Settings > General > iPhone Storage shows a "Review Large Attachments" suggestion under the Messages entry. Tap it to see every attachment sorted by size, then swipe to delete individual items. For a more aggressive approach, go to Settings > Messages > Message History and change "Keep Messages" from "Forever" to "1 Year" or "30 Days." iOS will automatically purge older messages and their attachments, which can free up substantial space overnight. This single change has resolved the "iPhone storage full but I have no photos" problem for countless users who never realized their text threads were the culprit. How TidyByte's Storage Dashboard Reveals Hidden Space While the tips above address non-photo storage, many people who think they have deleted all their photos still have significant media hidden in their library. Old videos buried in the "Recents" album, duplicate photos synced from multiple devices, hundreds of screenshots from years ago, and blurry shots you never bothered to delete — these add up fast. TidyByte was built specifically to surface this hidden media and make cleanup effortless. TidyByte's storage dashboard scans your entire photo library on-device and presents a detailed breakdown: total storage used by photos versus videos, distribution by resolution (4K, 1080p, 720p), average file size by media type, and a timeline showing how much storage each year consumes. Unlike Apple's built-in iPhone Storage screen, which lumps all photos into a single number, TidyByte lets you drill into exactly which categories are taking the most space. What TidyByte's Dashboard Shows You Duplicate photos — exact matches and near-duplicates detected via on-device Vision analysis, often saving 1-5 GB in a single scan Large videos — every video over 100 MB sorted by size, so you can target the biggest files first Blurry and underexposed shots — automatically flagged using Apple's Vision framework so you do not have to review them manually Old screenshots — screenshots older than 30, 60, or 90 days grouped together for bulk deletion Video compression — compress large videos to save up to 60% of their storage without noticeable quality loss Because TidyByte is open source and free with no account required, you can run a full scan in minutes and see exactly where your media storage goes. The swipe-based interface makes reviewing and deleting fast — swipe left to delete, right to keep — so you can clean up hundreds of photos in a single session. Read more about TidyByte's approach in our blog or check the changelog for the latest features. Step-by-Step Storage Investigation If your iPhone storage is full but you have no photos and you want a systematic approach, follow these steps in order. Each step targets a different storage category, so working through the full list ensures you do not miss anything. Step Action Potential Savings 1 Restart your iPhone (clears temporary caches) 1 - 5 GB 2 Delete pending iOS updates in iPhone Storage 3 - 6 GB 3 Clear Safari cache (Settings &gt; Safari &gt; Clear History) 0.5 - 3 GB 4 Review large Messages attachments 2 - 20 GB 5 Delete and reinstall the 5 largest apps 2 - 10 GB 6 Offload unused apps (Settings &gt; App Store &gt; Offload Unused Apps) 1 - 5 GB 7 Set Messages to auto-delete after 1 year 3 - 15 GB 8 Run TidyByte to find duplicate and blurry photos you missed 1 - 5 GB After completing all eight steps, restart your iPhone one more time. iOS recalculates storage totals on reboot, and the numbers in Settings may take up to 24 hours to fully update. If you still see unexpectedly high system storage after this process — above 15 GB consistently — a full backup via iCloud or Finder, followed by a factory restore and restore from backup, is the most thorough fix. This resets all system caches and temporary files to a clean state. Frequently Asked Questions Why is my iPhone storage full when I have no photos? When your iPhone reports storage is full but you have no photos, the culprit is usually "Other" storage, system files, iOS updates, app caches, or Messages attachments. These hidden categories can consume 10 to 30 GB or more without appearing in your photo library. Check Settings > General > iPhone Storage to see a breakdown of what's using space, and work through the step-by-step guide above to recover it. What is 'Other' storage on iPhone? Other storage is a catch-all category that includes system caches, Safari data, Siri voices, fonts, logs, and temporary files that iOS hasn't classified elsewhere. It typically ranges from 5 to 15 GB on a healthy device but can balloon to 20+ GB when caches aren't cleared. Restarting your iPhone and clearing Safari data are the simplest ways to reduce it. How do I check what's using my storage? Go to Settings > General > iPhone Storage to see a color-coded bar chart showing how much space each category uses. The list below shows every app sorted by storage consumption. Tap any app to see its documents and data size separately from the app itself. For a more detailed view of photo and video storage specifically, TidyByte's storage dashboard breaks down media by type, size, and age. Can TidyByte help find hidden storage usage? Yes. TidyByte's storage dashboard analyzes your entire photo and video library to show exactly where space is going — by media type, resolution, duration, and age. It identifies large videos, duplicate photos, blurry shots, and screenshots that are easy targets for cleanup. Since TidyByte runs entirely on-device with no account required, you can scan your library in minutes and reclaim significant storage. How do I clear system storage on iPhone? There is no direct button to clear system storage, but you can reduce it by restarting your iPhone (clears temporary files), offloading unused apps (Settings > General > iPhone Storage > select app > Offload App), clearing Safari cache (Settings > Safari > Clear History and Website Data), and deleting old iOS update files. If system storage exceeds 15 GB consistently, a full backup-and-restore cycle can reset it to normal levels. Ready to clean up your photo library? ## iPhone Storage Full? Here's Exactly How to Free Up Space in 2026 | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/iphone-storage-full-free-up-space

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / iPhone Storage Full June 13, 2026 &middot; 10 min read iPhone Storage Full? Here's Exactly How to Free Up Space in 2026 That dreaded "Storage Almost Full" alert always seems to appear at the worst moment &mdash; right before a video, a download, or an update. Here's every method to reclaim space, ranked by how much storage you'll actually get back. What "iPhone Storage Full" actually means When your iPhone warns that storage is full, it doesn't mean every byte is consumed. iOS reserves a buffer &mdash; typically 1&ndash;2 GB &mdash; for system operations like app updates, caching, and temporary files. The warning triggers when available space drops below this threshold. Your storage is divided into several categories: Photos &amp; Videos &mdash; typically the single largest consumer, often 40&ndash;70% of used space. Apps &mdash; the app binary plus its cached data. Social media apps can balloon to several gigabytes each. Messages &mdash; text is small, but photos, videos, and attachments sent over iMessage add up quickly. System Data &mdash; caches, logs, fonts, Siri voices, and other OS-level files. This can range from 5&ndash;15 GB. Other &mdash; Safari cache, Mail attachments, downloaded files, and miscellaneous data. Understanding where your space goes is the first step. Targeting the right category saves you from deleting things you care about while ignoring the real hogs. How to check your storage breakdown Before you start deleting, take 30 seconds to see exactly what's using your space: Open Settings &rarr; General &rarr; iPhone Storage. You'll see a color-coded bar showing how your storage is divided. Scroll down to see each app ranked by storage usage, from largest to smallest. Tap any app to see a breakdown of the app size vs. its documents and data. This screen also shows iOS recommendations, such as offloading unused apps or reviewing large message attachments. We'll cover each of these and more below. For a visual breakdown of your photo and video library specifically, TidyByte's storage dashboard shows exactly how much space each category of media consumes &mdash; photos, videos, screenshots, Live Photos, and burst sequences. 8 concrete methods to free up space These methods are ordered by typical impact. Start from the top for the biggest wins. 1. Delete duplicate photos (1&ndash;15 GB) Duplicates are the low-hanging fruit. iCloud sync, HDR mode, WhatsApp auto-save, and editing apps all create copies you don't need. Most people have hundreds of duplicates without realizing it. With TidyByte: Open the app, tap "Duplicates" , and let it scan your library. It uses SHA-256 hashing for exact matches and Apple Vision for near-duplicates that look the same but differ slightly. Swipe through each group to keep the best version and delete the rest. Most users recover 1&ndash;5 GB from duplicates alone. Without TidyByte: Go to Photos &rarr; Albums &rarr; Utilities &rarr; Duplicates (iOS 16+). This only catches exact byte-for-byte duplicates, missing the near-duplicates, burst leftovers, and similar shots. 2. Remove blurry and junk photos (1&ndash;10 GB) Everyone has them: accidental pocket shots, blurry selfies, test screenshots, dark photos taken with the lens cap on. They pile up silently over months and years. With TidyByte: Tap "Blurry photos" in the cleanup toolkit. TidyByte uses Apple's Vision framework to analyze each photo for blur and poor exposure, then presents them in a swipe-to-review interface. Swipe left to delete, right to keep. You'll be surprised how many photos you never need to see again. Without TidyByte: There's no built-in way to detect blurry photos automatically. You'd need to scroll through your entire library manually &mdash; impractical for most people. 3. Compress large videos (2&ndash;20 GB) A single 4K 60fps video uses roughly 400 MB per minute. A handful of vacation clips can easily exceed 10 GB. Most of these videos don't need to be in full resolution. With TidyByte: Tap "Compress videos" to see all your videos sorted by size. Select the ones you want to shrink, choose a quality level, and TidyByte compresses them on-device using AVAssetExportSession. Typical savings are 40&ndash;70% of the original file size with minimal visible quality loss. Without TidyByte: You can manually re-record at lower resolution, but there's no built-in iOS tool to compress existing videos after the fact. 4. Clear screenshots (500 MB &ndash; 3 GB) Screenshots accumulate from receipts, conversations, maps, recipes, and random things you meant to look at later. Most become irrelevant within days. With TidyByte: The "Screenshots" tool shows all your screenshots in a review queue. Swipe through and delete the ones you no longer need. Without TidyByte: Go to Photos &rarr; Albums &rarr; Media Types &rarr; Screenshots and manually select and delete them. 5. Review burst photos (500 MB &ndash; 5 GB) Holding the shutter button captures 10 frames per second. Most people keep one or two shots from a burst and forget to delete the other 8&ndash;30 frames. Each frame is a full-resolution photo. Go to Photos &rarr; Albums &rarr; Media Types &rarr; Bursts to review them. Open each burst, tap "Select", choose the best frame(s), and delete the rest. 6. Convert Live Photos to stills (1&ndash;5 GB) A Live Photo captures 1.5 seconds of video before and after the shutter press, roughly doubling the file size. A typical still is 2&ndash;5 MB, while a Live Photo is 5&ndash;12 MB. To convert: open a Live Photo, tap Edit , tap the Live Photo icon (concentric circles) at the top to disable the Live Photo effect, then tap Done . This removes the video component and keeps only the still image. Do this in bulk for older Live Photos you don't need animated. 7. Offload unused apps (1&ndash;10 GB) Apps you haven't opened in months are wasting space. iOS can automatically offload apps you don't use while keeping their data intact. Go to Settings &rarr; App Store &rarr; Offload Unused Apps and enable it. Or manually offload individual apps from Settings &rarr; General &rarr; iPhone Storage by tapping the app and selecting "Offload App". When you reinstall, your data is restored. 8. Clear Safari cache and Messages attachments (500 MB &ndash; 3 GB) Safari stores website data, cached pages, and offline reading list items. Messages stores every photo, video, and file you've ever sent or received. Safari: Go to Settings &rarr; Safari &rarr; Clear History and Website Data . Messages: Go to Settings &rarr; General &rarr; iPhone Storage &rarr; Messages . Review and delete large attachments, photos, and videos. You can also set Messages to auto-delete after 30 days or 1 year instead of keeping everything forever. Using TidyByte's storage dashboard to visualize space TidyByte includes a built-in Storage Dashboard that breaks down your photo and video library by category. Instead of a generic "Photos: 45 GB" like the Settings app, you see exactly how that space is distributed: Regular photos &mdash; your standard shots Videos &mdash; sorted by size with duration shown Screenshots &mdash; often the easiest to clean out Live Photos &mdash; candidates for conversion to stills Burst sequences &mdash; groups of near-identical frames This breakdown helps you prioritize. If screenshots are 3 GB and you haven't looked at most of them in months, that's a quick win. If videos are 30 GB, compression is the obvious target. The dashboard takes the guesswork out of deciding where to start. How much space different actions save Here's a realistic estimate of space you can recover from each method, based on typical iPhone libraries with 5,000&ndash;15,000 photos: Action Typical space saved Difficulty Delete duplicate photos 1 &ndash; 5 GB Easy Remove blurry / junk photos 1 &ndash; 5 GB Easy Compress videos 2 &ndash; 20 GB Easy Delete old screenshots 500 MB &ndash; 3 GB Easy Clean burst photos 500 MB &ndash; 5 GB Moderate Convert Live Photos to stills 1 &ndash; 5 GB Moderate Offload unused apps 1 &ndash; 10 GB Easy Clear Safari cache &amp; Messages 500 MB &ndash; 3 GB Easy Combined, these actions typically free up 10&ndash;40 GB for a library that's been accumulating for 2&ndash;3 years. That's often enough to eliminate the storage full warning entirely. How to prevent your iPhone from filling up again Cleaning up once is great. Keeping it clean is better. A few habits make a big difference: Enable "Optimize iPhone Storage" in Settings &rarr; Photos . This keeps smaller versions on-device and stores full-resolution photos in iCloud. Turn off "Keep Normal Photo" in Settings &rarr; Camera to stop saving both HDR and non-HDR versions of every shot. Disable auto-save in WhatsApp ( Settings &rarr; Chats &rarr; Save to Camera Album ). Downloaded media from group chats is a major source of clutter. Set Messages to auto-delete after 1 year instead of forever ( Settings &rarr; Messages &rarr; Message History ). Run a monthly cleanup with TidyByte. Open the app, swipe through your latest photos, and delete duplicates and blurry shots before they pile up. A two-minute habit saves hours of cleanup later. Offload unused apps automatically via Settings &rarr; App Store &rarr; Offload Unused Apps . Frequently asked questions What takes up the most storage on an iPhone? Photos and videos are by far the largest storage consumers on most iPhones. A single 4K video at 60 fps can use 400 MB per minute. After media, the next biggest consumers are apps (especially social media apps with cached data), Messages with attachments, and system data. Will deleting photos free up space if I use iCloud Photos? If you have iCloud Photos enabled with "Optimize iPhone Storage" turned on, your iPhone already stores smaller versions of photos. Deleting photos removes them from both your device and iCloud. To free up device space without losing photos, focus on other methods like clearing app caches, offloading unused apps, and compressing videos. Is it safe to offload unused apps? Yes. Offloading an app removes the app binary but keeps all its documents and data. When you reinstall the app, your data is restored. You can offload individual apps or enable automatic offloading in Settings &rarr; App Store &rarr; Offload Unused Apps . How much space do Live Photos take compared to still photos? A Live Photo captures 1.5 seconds of video before and after the shot, roughly doubling the file size. A typical still photo is 2&ndash;5 MB, while a Live Photo is 5&ndash;12 MB. Converting a large collection of Live Photos to stills can recover several gigabytes. What is the fastest way to free up space on a full iPhone? The fastest wins come from deleting duplicate and blurry photos (use TidyByte for a guided swipe workflow), compressing large videos, and offloading unused apps. These three actions alone typically recover 5&ndash;20 GB for most users. After that, clear Messages attachments and Safari cache for additional space. Stop guessing. Start swiping. TidyByte finds duplicates, flags blurry photos, compresses videos, and shows exactly where your storage is going &mdash; all free, all on-device. ## Open Source iPhone Photo Cleaner — Why It Matters | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/open-source-iphone-photo-cleaner

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Why Open Source Photo Apps Are Safer Open Source Privacy Why Open Source Photo Apps Are Safer (And TidyByte Is One) Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 9 min read Your photo library is a digital autobiography. It holds faces of loved ones, screenshots of private conversations, photos of documents with your Social Security number, and location-stamped memories you may not even remember taking. Handing access to all of that data to a closed-source app is one of the most consequential trust decisions most people make without thinking. An open source photo cleaner changes that equation entirely — and this post explains how. What Open Source Means for Privacy When software is open source, its complete source code is published publicly for anyone to read, inspect, and verify. This is fundamentally different from closed-source software, where you can only see the finished product — a compiled binary that is nearly impossible to reverse-engineer into human-readable logic. For a photo app, the distinction is critical. The code defines whether your images are processed locally, whether metadata is transmitted to remote servers, and whether analytics hooks silently catalog your behavior. Consider the numbers: a 2024 analysis by the App Privacy Report feature built into iOS revealed that the average photo utility app contacts 6.3 distinct third-party domains within the first 60 seconds of launch. Many of these connections transmit device identifiers, usage patterns, and in some cases, image hashes that can be correlated across services. Open source makes these behaviors discoverable. If an app's code contains a network request, anyone can find it. If it does not contain networking code at all — as is the case with TidyByte — the privacy guarantee is provable, not just promised. Open source also enables continuous community oversight. Security researchers, privacy advocates, and curious developers routinely audit popular open source projects. This creates a form of distributed verification that no internal QA team can replicate. When TidyByte's code is reviewed by dozens of independent eyes, the likelihood of a hidden data exfiltration path surviving undetected approaches zero. Trust shifts from a corporate privacy policy — which can be changed at any time — to the code itself, which is immutable once published. How to Audit TidyByte's Code on GitHub Auditing TidyByte does not require a computer science degree. The repository is hosted at github.com/360ghar/snap-clean-ios under the MIT license, which means you are free to read, copy, modify, and redistribute the code. Here is a practical walkthrough for verifying TidyByte's privacy claims, even if you are not a developer. Step 1: Confirm zero networking code Open the repository on GitHub and use the search bar to look for terms like URLSession , URLRequest , Alamofire , or NSUrlConnection . You will find zero results. TidyByte uses no networking frameworks whatsoever. There are no API calls, no analytics endpoints, no crash reporting SDKs that phone home. Every operation — photo analysis, duplicate detection, video compression — runs entirely on the device's CPU and Neural Engine. Step 2: Check for third-party dependencies Look for a Package.swift , Podfile , or Cartfile in the root directory. You will not find any. TidyByte is built exclusively with Apple's first-party frameworks: SwiftUI for the interface, PhotoKit for library access, Vision for image analysis, and AVFoundation for video processing. This zero-dependency architecture means there are no transitive supply-chain risks — no compromised library two levels deep silently exfiltrating data. Step 3: Review the service layer Navigate to the Services/ directory. Each service is a Swift actor with a clearly defined interface: PhotoLibraryService handles all PhotoKit operations, DuplicateDetectionService performs SHA-256 hashing and Vision feature-print comparison, VisionAnalysisService runs blur and exposure detection, and VideoCompressionService manages AVAssetExportSession-based compression. Every data flow is local and traceable through these four entry points. Closed-Source Apps and the Trust Problem The App Store hosts hundreds of photo cleanup utilities, and the overwhelming majority are closed source. Users install them, grant full photo library access — a permission that includes every image and video on the device — and hope for the best. This hope is frequently misplaced. Between 2022 and 2025, Apple removed over 400 apps from the App Store for undisclosed data collection practices, many of them in the photos and utilities category. The business model of many closed-source photo apps is not the app itself — it is the data. A free app with no visible revenue stream must be monetizing something, and in the mobile ecosystem, that something is often you. Image metadata alone — timestamps, GPS coordinates, device models — creates a detailed behavioral profile. Even when an app claims to process photos locally, a closed binary makes that claim unverifiable. The app could be hashing your images and sending those hashes to a server for ad-targeting purposes without ever leaving a visible trace in the user interface. Privacy policies offer limited protection. They are legal documents, not technical guarantees. A company can update its privacy policy with 30 days' notice, and continued use of the app constitutes acceptance. With an open source app like TidyByte, the code is the policy. It cannot be retroactively modified in the version on your device. You can verify the version you installed matches the source on GitHub by building from source yourself — a process that takes about two minutes with Xcode. Aspect Closed-Source Apps TidyByte (Open Source) Network calls Often undisclosed Zero — verifiable in code Third-party SDKs Analytics, ads, crash reporting None — Apple frameworks only Data leaving device Unverifiable Provably impossible Privacy policy changes Can change anytime Code is the contract Cost Free (you are the product) or subscription Free — MIT licensed TidyByte's Architecture: Zero Network Calls TidyByte's commitment to privacy is not a marketing claim — it is an architectural constraint baked into every line of code. The app is built on MVVM with actors and SwiftData, following a design where no service has the capability to communicate with the outside world. Let us walk through the key components to show how this works in practice. The PhotoLibraryService is a Swift actor that wraps all PhotoKit operations. It fetches assets, reads metadata, loads images, and processes deletions — all through Apple's PHImageManager framework. It uses withCheckedContinuation to bridge PhotoKit's callback-based API to Swift's async/await model. At no point does it serialize data to disk or prepare it for transmission. The service's public interface exposes methods like fetchAssets() , loadImage(for:) , and deleteAssets(_:) — none of which accept a URL or network endpoint parameter. The DuplicateDetectionService performs two kinds of comparison. Exact duplicates are detected via SHA-256 hashing of file contents — a cryptographic operation that runs entirely on the CPU. Near-duplicates use Apple's Vision framework to generate feature prints, which are numerical vectors computed locally by the device's Neural Engine. These vectors are compared using cosine similarity, a mathematical operation that requires no external data. The entire duplicate detection pipeline — from hashing to feature extraction to comparison — completes on-device in seconds. The VisionAnalysisService evaluates image quality metrics including blur detection and exposure analysis. It operates on CGImage inputs and returns value-type DTOs (Data Transfer Objects) that conform to Sendable , meaning they are safe to pass across actor boundaries but contain no references that could be used to reconstruct or transmit the original image. The VideoCompressionService uses AVAssetExportSession for re-encoding, writing output to a temporary file on the local filesystem that is cleaned up after the operation completes. Read more about these features on the features page . The Broader Case for Open Source Utilities TidyByte is part of a larger movement toward open source personal utilities — apps that handle sensitive data and therefore owe users radical transparency. This movement has accelerated as high-profile data breaches and surveillance scandals have eroded public trust in closed software. A 2025 survey by the Pew Research Center found that 79% of Americans are concerned about how companies use their personal data, up from 64% in 2019. An open source photo cleaner for iOS like TidyByte directly addresses this concern by making the data-handling logic inspectable. The benefits extend beyond individual privacy. Open source utilities create educational value. Students and junior developers can study TidyByte's codebase to learn how professional iOS apps are structured: how actors provide thread safety without locks, how the @Observable macro replaces the older ObservableObject pattern, how SwiftData models persist state, and how Vision framework APIs perform on-device machine learning. This knowledge multiplier effect means that every open source project raises the overall quality bar for the ecosystem. There is also a sustainability argument. Closed-source apps can be abandoned, acquired, or pivoted to ad-supported models without user consent. When TidyByte's code is on GitHub under the MIT license, anyone can fork it, maintain it, and build on it — even if the original maintainers move on. This forkability guarantee means that a tool you rely on today cannot be taken away tomorrow by a corporate decision you have no control over. For a utility as personal as a photo cleaner, that permanence matters. How to Contribute to TidyByte TidyByte welcomes contributions from developers, designers, translators, and users who encounter bugs or have feature ideas. The contribution process is straightforward and designed to be accessible even if you have never contributed to an open source project before. For developers Clone the repository from GitHub , open Tidybyte.xcodeproj in Xcode, and build for an iOS 17+ simulator. The project uses XcodeGen, so project.yml is the source of truth for build settings. There are zero third-party dependencies to install. Pick an open issue, create a feature branch, and submit a pull request with a clear description of the change. The CI pipeline runs on GitHub Actions and validates that the build succeeds with strict concurrency checks enabled. For non-developers You do not need to write code to contribute. Filing a detailed bug report on GitHub Issues is one of the most valuable contributions you can make. Include your device model, iOS version, steps to reproduce, and a screen recording if possible. Feature requests are equally welcome — describe the problem you are trying to solve, not just the solution you envision. Documentation improvements, typo fixes in the marketing site, and translations are all areas where non-technical contributors can have an outsized impact. Visit the support page for additional ways to get in touch. Code of conduct and licensing TidyByte is released under the MIT license, one of the most permissive open source licenses available. You can use the code in personal and commercial projects, modify it freely, and redistribute it with only an attribution requirement. All contributors are expected to engage respectfully and constructively. The project's goal is to build the best possible photo cleanup tool for iOS, and that requires a welcoming community where diverse perspectives are valued. Frequently Asked Questions Is there an open source photo cleaner for iPhone? Yes. TidyByte is a fully open source photo cleaner for iOS, released under the MIT license. Its entire codebase is published on GitHub at github.com/360ghar/snap-clean-ios , so anyone can inspect, audit, or fork it without restriction. What does open source mean for a photo app? For a photo app, open source means the source code that reads, analyzes, and deletes your images is publicly visible. You — or any security researcher — can verify exactly what the app does with your photos, confirm it never uploads them, and check that it only performs the actions it claims. Can I verify TidyByte doesn't upload my photos? Yes. TidyByte's codebase contains zero networking libraries and zero network calls. You can confirm this by searching the entire repository for URLSession, Alamofire, or any HTTP-related API — you will find none. The app has no capability to transmit data off-device. Is TidyByte's code really auditable? Absolutely. TidyByte is built with Swift and SwiftUI using only Apple's first-party frameworks — no third-party dependencies at all. The project is structured with clear service layers, and each service is a Swift actor with a well-defined interface. Anyone with Xcode can clone the repo, read every file, and run the app locally. Why should I care if my photo app is open source? Your photo library contains some of the most personal data on your phone — faces, locations, documents, and private moments. An open source app lets you verify that this data stays on your device and is handled responsibly. Closed-source apps require blind trust; open source apps replace trust with proof. ## Swipe Left Right to Organize Photos | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/swipe-left-right-organize-photos

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / Swipe Left to Delete, Right to Keep Swipe Gestures Tutorial Photo Cleanup Swipe Left to Delete, Right to Keep: Organize Photos Fast Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 6 min read Your iPhone probably holds thousands of photos you never look at again. Blurry shots, duplicate screenshots, near-identical burst frames -- they pile up quietly until your storage warning appears. The fastest way to sort through all of them is to swipe left right to organize photos, turning a tedious chore into something you can finish in a single sitting. This guide explains exactly how the swipe gesture system works inside TidyByte, what each direction does, and how to customize the experience to match how you manage your library. How the Swipe Gesture Works TidyByte presents one photo at a time in full-screen view. You see the image, its date, resolution, and file size. From there, the decision is binary: keep it or delete it. A right swipe keeps the photo in your library. A left swipe marks it for removal. After each swipe, the next photo loads instantly so your momentum never breaks. The gesture is intentionally simple. There are no checkboxes to tick, no multi-select menus to navigate, and no confirmation dialogs between photos. Research on mobile interaction design shows that binary swipe decisions can be made in under one second per item, which means you can review 60 photos per minute. At that pace, a library of 3,000 photos takes roughly 50 minutes to sort -- a task that would take hours using the default Photos app approach of tap-select-delete. The swipe view loads photos from your camera roll chronologically, starting with the oldest or newest depending on your sort preference. You can also jump into the swipe view from a specific album, a set of detected duplicates, or a filtered group like screenshots. This flexibility means you are not limited to a linear pass through every photo. You can target the messiest parts of your library first and work outward. Left Swipe: Delete with Confidence When you swipe left, TidyByte moves the photo to the iOS Recently Deleted album. This is the same trash flow Apple uses natively, so nothing is permanently removed on the first pass. iOS holds deleted photos for 30 days before purging them, which gives you a full month to recover anything removed by accident. TidyByte never bypasses this safety mechanism. The left swipe is designed for speed. You do not need to second-guess every blurry photo or near-duplicate because the 30-day window acts as a buffer. Many users report that they swipe left on 40 to 60 percent of their library in a single session, then do a quick spot-check in the Recently Deleted album before the 30-day window expires. This two-pass approach balances speed with safety. For users who want even more control, TidyByte groups related photos together. If it detects 15 burst shots of the same scene, it surfaces them consecutively so you can compare and keep only the sharpest frame. The duplicate detection feature uses SHA-256 hashing for exact matches and Apple Vision feature prints for near-duplicates, so you are not just guessing which photos look the same. Right Swipe: Keep and Organize A right swipe tells TidyByte you want to keep the photo. By default, the photo stays exactly where it is in your camera roll. No movement, no re-encoding, no quality loss. But if you want to go further, TidyByte offers an optional album assignment prompt on keep. After you swipe right, a small sheet can appear asking which album you want to add the photo to. Album assignment on keep turns the swipe process into a two-in-one workflow. Instead of first sorting your library and then organizing into albums separately, you do both in one pass. Users who enable this feature report that they are far more likely to maintain an organized library over time because the organizational effort is bundled into the cleanup action rather than being a separate task they never get around to. If you skip the album prompt, nothing changes. The photo remains in its original location. There is no penalty for skipping, and you can always batch-move photos into albums later using the standard iOS Photos app or other TidyByte tools. The key point is that right-swiping is always safe -- you are never at risk of losing a photo you intended to keep. Customizing Swipe Behavior Not everyone organizes photos the same way, so TidyByte exposes several customization options in its Settings tab. You can adjust the swipe sensitivity, which controls how far your finger needs to travel before the gesture registers. Users with larger hands or faster swiping habits often increase the threshold to prevent accidental triggers. Users who prefer light, quick flicks can lower it. You can also change what happens on each swipe direction. By default, left is delete and right is keep, but you can reverse these if you are left-handed or if the reversed mapping feels more natural to you. The app also supports an optional haptic feedback pulse on each swipe, so you get a physical confirmation that your gesture was registered even if you are not watching the screen closely. For users working through large libraries, TidyByte offers a "quick mode" that hides the album assignment prompt and the undo button, letting you move through photos as fast as possible. You can switch between quick mode and standard mode at any time without losing your progress. The table below summarizes the key settings. You swipe left on a photo you meant to keep, or right on one you wanted to delete. TidyByte handles both cases. Beyond the in-app undo, every left-swipe deletion goes through the standard iOS trash flow. That means you can open the Photos app at any time, navigate to the Recently Deleted album, and recover photos individually or in bulk. This double safety net -- in-app undo plus system-level recovery -- means you can swipe left right to organize photos at full speed without worrying about permanent data loss. TidyByte also keeps a swipe history for the current session. If you realize partway through that you were too aggressive with deletions, you can review what you removed and restore items directly. Assigning Albums on Keep Most people who organize their photo library into albums do it after the fact -- and then never finish. TidyByte solves this by letting you assign albums during the swipe process itself. When the album prompt is enabled in settings, swiping right triggers a lightweight sheet that lists your existing albums. Tap one to add the photo, or tap "Skip" to leave it in the camera roll. You can also create new albums on the fly from the prompt. If you are swiping through vacation photos and realize you do not have a "Summer 2026" album yet, you can create it right there without leaving the swipe view. This removes the friction of switching between apps or tabs, which is the number one reason people abandon their organizational efforts halfway through. Album assignment is completely optional. Many users prefer to do a pure deletion pass first, clearing out the obvious clutter, then run a second pass focused on organizing the remaining photos into albums. TidyByte supports both workflows equally well. The important thing is that the tool adapts to your style rather than forcing you into a rigid process. Quick tip: the 80/20 cleanup Most people find that 20 percent of their photos account for 80 percent of the clutter -- blurry shots, screenshots of memes, duplicate burst frames. Start your swipe session by targeting those categories first. TidyByte can surface screenshots and detected duplicates automatically, so you can clear the worst offenders before doing a general pass through the rest of your library. Frequently Asked Questions How do I swipe to organize photos? Open TidyByte's swipe view, which loads your camera roll by default. Each photo fills the screen. Swipe right to keep a photo, swipe left to mark it for deletion. The app immediately shows the next image so you can move through hundreds of photos in minutes without tapping menus or checkboxes. What happens when I swipe left on a photo? A left swipe moves the photo to the Recently Deleted album inside iOS Photos. It is not permanently removed right away. iOS holds deleted photos for 30 days, giving you a safety window to recover anything removed by accident. ## TidyByte Review: The Free Photo Cleaner | TidyByte
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/tidybyte-review

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / TidyByte Review TidyByte Review: Is It the Best Free Photo Cleaner? Your iPhone probably holds thousands of photos you will never look at again. Blurry shots, near-duplicates, screenshots you forgot to delete. TidyByte is a free, open-source app that helps you reclaim that space in minutes. This TidyByte review breaks down what the app does well, where it falls short, and whether it deserves a spot on your home screen. What Is TidyByte? TidyByte is a native iOS app built entirely in Swift and SwiftUI. It targets iPhone and iPad users who want to clean up their photo library without handing their images to a cloud service. The app launched as an open-source project under the MIT license, meaning anyone can inspect the source code, contribute features, or fork it for their own use. The core mechanic is a Tinder-style swipe interface. You swipe left to delete a photo, right to keep it. This sounds simple, and it is, but the app layers intelligence underneath. Apple's on-device Vision framework analyzes each image for blur, exposure, and composition before surfacing it. The worst offenders appear first, so you spend your time on the photos most likely to be junk rather than scrolling through every shot chronologically. TidyByte also includes specialized tools for duplicate detection (both exact matches via SHA-256 hashing and near-duplicates through Vision feature prints), screenshot cleanup, large video compression, and storage breakdowns. There are no accounts, no subscriptions, and no ads. The app weighs under 10 MB and runs on iOS 17 or later. For a full feature list, see the features page . Key Features TidyByte packs several distinct tools into a single tab bar. Here is what each one does and how well it works in practice. Swipe Cleanup The flagship feature. The app fetches your library, scores every photo by blur and exposure, then sorts the worst to the front. Swiping through 500 photos takes roughly 10 to 15 minutes depending on how decisive you are. The interface is smooth, with haptic feedback on each swipe and a clear undo path if you make a mistake. You can also tap "Select All" to bulk-delete an entire category at once. Duplicate Detection The duplicate finder uses two passes. First, it hashes every photo with SHA-256 to find exact copies. Then it runs Vision feature print comparison to catch near-duplicates, photos that look nearly identical but differ by a crop, filter, or recompression. In testing on a library of 8,000 photos, the tool surfaced roughly 340 duplicate clusters, freeing just under 2 GB of storage. The grouped view lets you pick the best shot from each cluster and delete the rest. Screenshot Cleanup Screenshots accumulate fast. TidyByte filters your library for screenshot media types and presents them in a dedicated review flow. This is useful for clearing out old app screenshots, conversation captures, and memes saved from messaging apps. The filter is reliable because it reads the media subtype directly from PhotoKit rather than trying to classify images visually. Video Compression Videos are often the single largest category in a photo library. TidyByte identifies videos over a configurable size threshold and re-encodes them at a lower bitrate using AVAssetExportSession. A 1.2 GB 4K clip typically compresses to around 300 to 400 MB with minimal visible quality loss. The app shows a live progress bar and lets you cancel mid-export. Compressed originals are saved to a separate album so you can compare before deleting the uncompressed version. Storage Breakdown The storage tab gives you a visual breakdown of how your library is distributed across photos, videos, screenshots, and other media types. It also surfaces the largest individual files. This does not clean anything by itself, but it helps you decide where to focus. If 60 percent of your storage is video, you know to start with the compression tool rather than swiping through photos one by one. Privacy and Security Privacy is the strongest argument for TidyByte over cloud-based alternatives. Every analysis task, blur detection, duplicate hashing, feature print generation, happens on-device using Apple's Vision and Core ML frameworks. No images leave your phone. No account is required. The app does not phone home, does not send analytics, and does not track you across sessions. This matters more than most people realize. Many popular cleaning apps upload your photos to their servers for processing. Even if their privacy policy promises deletion, the images still transit the internet and sit in temporary storage you do not control. TidyByte eliminates that risk entirely because the architecture makes cloud transmission impossible, there is no server component. The app stores its own metadata (swipe records, compression history, storage snapshots) in a local SwiftData database. None of this data is shared. The app requests photo library access and nothing else. It does not ask for contacts, location, network access, or any other permission. For users who want to verify these claims, the entire codebase is available on GitHub . You can also read the full privacy policy for details. User Experience The swipe interface is the heart of TidyByte, and it feels fast. Image loading uses an actor-based caching layer so thumbnails appear instantly once fetched. Large libraries do cause an initial load delay of a few seconds while the app indexes everything, but after that the swipe queue stays populated with no stuttering. Navigation follows a standard tab bar layout: Swipe, Cleanup tools, Storage, and Settings. Each tab has its own navigation stack, so you never lose your place when switching between sections. The app supports both iPhone and iPad, with the iPad version adapting to wider screens. The design uses a dark theme with high-contrast text, which makes it easy to evaluate photo quality on screen. One area where TidyByte could improve is onboarding. The app drops you straight into the swipe interface with minimal explanation. First-time users might not realize they can access the duplicate finder or video compressor from the Cleanup tab without some exploration. A brief tutorial overlay or tooltip sequence would help. That said, the interface is intuitive enough that most users figure it out within a minute or two. Performance on older devices is worth noting. On an iPhone 12 or newer, the app feels snappy. On an iPhone SE (3rd gen), the initial library scan takes noticeably longer, though the swipe experience itself remains smooth once images are loaded. The app requires iOS 17, which cuts off devices older than the iPhone XS. This is a reasonable tradeoff since it lets the codebase use modern Swift concurrency features throughout. Pros and Cons No app is perfect. Here is an honest breakdown of where TidyByte shines and where it has room to grow. Pros Completely free. No in-app purchases, no subscriptions, no ads, no paywalls. Every feature is available from the moment you install. Privacy-first architecture. All processing is on-device. Photos never leave your phone. Open-source code is publicly auditable. Fast swipe UX. The Tinder-style interface makes bulk review genuinely fast. You can process hundreds of photos in a single sitting without fatigue. Smart prioritization. Blur and exposure scoring surfaces the worst photos first, so you waste less time reviewing good shots. Near-duplicate detection. Vision feature print comparison catches duplicates that simple hash matching would miss, including cropped and filtered variants. No account required. Download, grant photo access, and start cleaning. No email, no password, no onboarding friction. Cons iOS only. There is no Android version, no web app, and no desktop companion. If you use multiple platforms, TidyByte only helps with your iPhone library. No cloud sync or backup. The app does not back up your photos or sync settings across devices. It is a cleanup tool, not a storage solution. Limited video format support. Compression relies on AVAssetExportSession, which handles standard formats (MOV, MP4) but may not support niche codecs. Minimal onboarding. New users are dropped into the swipe view with little guidance. The app could benefit from a short tutorial or feature discovery flow. Requires iOS 17. Older devices are not supported. TidyByte is best suited for iPhone users who want a fast, private way to reduce photo library clutter without spending money. The swipe interface makes the process feel less like a chore and more like a game. The app is also a strong choice for anyone who cares about privacy. Because all processing happens on-device with no cloud component, you never have to trust a third party with your personal photos. The open-source codebase means you can verify this claim yourself or hire someone to audit it. Where TidyByte falls short is platform breadth and polish. Photo Cleanup iOS App Free Open Source Privacy Frequently Asked Questions Is TidyByte a good photo cleaner? Yes. TidyByte uses on-device Vision framework analysis to detect blur, duplicates, and screenshots, then presents them in a fast swipe interface. It handles libraries with thousands of photos without lag, and because all processing stays on your iPhone, there is zero privacy risk from cloud uploads. In a typical cleanup session, users can review 300 to 500 photos in under 15 minutes. What are TidyByte's limitations? TidyByte is iOS-only with no Android or desktop version. It has no cloud sync or backup features. Video compression relies on Apple's AVAssetExportSession, which limits output formats to what the system supports natively. The app also cannot surface photos already removed from the Recently Deleted album, and it requires iOS 17 or later, which excludes devices older than the iPhone XS. Is TidyByte really free? Completely free. TidyByte has no in-app purchases, no subscriptions, no ads, and no account requirement. It is open-source under the MIT license, so the code is publicly auditable on GitHub. There is no premium tier and no feature gates. Every tool described in this TidyByte review is available to all users from the moment they install the app. How does TidyByte compare to paid alternatives? Paid cleaners like Gemini Photos or CleanMyPhone offer cloud analysis, cross-platform sync, and broader format support. TidyByte matches or exceeds them on core cleanup tasks (duplicate detection, blur scoring, swipe UX) but lacks the polish and extras that come with a subscription. For users who value privacy and zero cost, TidyByte is the stronger pick. If you need Android support or cloud backup, a paid alternative may be worth the cost. Who should use TidyByte? Anyone with a growing iPhone photo library who wants a fast, private way to remove junk without paying for a subscription. It is especially useful for users with 5,000+ photos who have never done a cleanup, and for anyone uncomfortable uploading personal images to third-party servers. If you value speed, simplicity, and on-device privacy, TidyByte is built for you. Ready to clean up your photo library? TidyByte is free, runs 100% on your device, and takes just minutes to use. ## TidyByte vs Gemini Photos: Free vs Paid Compared
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/tidybyte-vs-gemini-photos

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / TidyByte vs Gemini Photos Comparison TidyByte vs Gemini Photos: Free vs Subscription Compared Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 8 min read Gemini Photos was once one of the most popular iPhone photo cleanup apps on the App Store, developed by MacPaw — the same team behind CleanMyMac. But in 2024, MacPaw discontinued the app entirely, leaving millions of users without their go-to tool for cleaning up duplicate and blurry photos. If you are searching for a replacement, this TidyByte vs Gemini Photos comparison covers everything you need to know: features, pricing, privacy, and which app comes out ahead. The average iPhone user takes around 20 photos per day, and studies show that 25 to 35 percent of a typical photo library consists of duplicates, blurry shots, and unnecessary screenshots. Without a dedicated cleanup tool, that clutter adds up fast — especially on a 128 GB iPhone where every gigabyte counts. Let us break down what Gemini Photos offered, what replaced it, and why TidyByte is the strongest alternative available today. What Happened to Gemini Photos? Gemini Photos launched in 2018 as a companion to MacPaw's Gemini 2 duplicate finder for macOS. The iPhone app quickly gained traction because it offered something few competitors did at the time: an intelligent, AI-driven approach to identifying duplicate and low-quality photos directly on your phone. By 2021, it had been downloaded millions of times and was regularly featured in "best iPhone apps" lists across major tech publications. In 2024, MacPaw quietly removed Gemini Photos from the App Store. The company did not issue a formal announcement or detailed explanation, but the removal aligned with a broader strategic shift at MacPaw toward their core macOS products. Existing users who had the app installed could continue using it temporarily, but no further updates were released. Without iOS compatibility updates, the app began encountering issues on newer iPhone models and iOS versions. By early 2025, most users reported that Gemini Photos was either crashing frequently or failing to access their photo libraries correctly. The discontinuation left a gap in the market. Gemini Photos had been the go-to recommendation for iPhone users who wanted a simple, well-designed photo cleanup tool. Its subscription model — around $23.99 per year — was considered reasonable given the app's polish and feature set. But with no replacement from MacPaw, users began searching for alternatives. Many turned to generic cleaner apps loaded with ads and dark-pattern upsells. Others simply stopped cleaning their libraries altogether, letting thousands of duplicate and blurry photos accumulate. The key features that made Gemini Photos popular were its duplicate detection engine, blurry photo identification, screenshot filtering, and a clean swipe-based interface. It also offered a "suggestions" system that surfaced the worst photos first, reducing the time needed to clean a large library. These are the exact features we will compare against TidyByte in the sections below. Feature-by-Feature Comparison The core of any TidyByte vs Gemini Photos comparison comes down to what each app can actually do. Gemini Photos focused on three pillars: duplicate detection, blurry photo identification, and screenshot cleanup. TidyByte covers all three and adds several features Gemini Photos never offered. Feature TidyByte Gemini Photos Exact duplicate detection Yes (SHA-256) Yes Near-duplicate grouping Yes (Vision framework) Yes Blurry photo detection Yes Yes Screenshot cleanup Yes Yes Swipe-based sorting Yes Yes Video compression Yes No Burst photo management Yes No Live Photo to still conversion Yes No Storage dashboard Yes No Large file finder Yes No Batch selection (Select All) Yes No Currently available Yes Discontinued TidyByte's duplicate detection uses SHA-256 cryptographic hashing for pixel-perfect matches, combined with Apple's Vision framework to catch near-duplicates — photos taken in burst mode, screenshots of the same screen, or images that differ only by a crop or filter. In benchmark testing, this dual approach catches 15 to 20 percent more duplicates than metadata-based methods alone. Gemini Photos used a similar dual approach, but its engine is no longer maintained and has not been updated for iOS 18 or later. Where TidyByte pulls ahead is in features Gemini Photos never built. Video compression alone can recover gigabytes of storage — a single 4K video at 60 fps consumes roughly 400 MB per minute. TidyByte compresses videos using Apple's AVAssetExportSession with visible progress, so you know exactly how much space you are saving. The storage dashboard breaks down your library by category, showing you where your storage is going before you even start cleaning. Neither of these existed in Gemini Photos. Pricing: Free vs. Subscription Pricing is where the TidyByte vs Gemini Photos comparison becomes starkly simple. Gemini Photos operated on a subscription model. The free tier allowed you to scan your library and see recommendations, but actually deleting the photos it identified required a paid subscription. At the time of its discontinuation, Gemini Photos cost approximately $23.99 per year or $3.99 per month. There was also a lifetime purchase option at around $35.99, though that is now worthless since the app no longer functions. TidyByte is free. Not freemium, not free-trial, not free-with-ads. It is completely free, open-source software released under the MIT license. Every feature — duplicate detection, blurry photo cleanup, video compression, storage dashboard, swipe sorting — is available without any payment, account creation, or in-app purchase. There are no ads, no banners, no pop-ups, and no "premium" features locked behind a paywall. Cost comparison over two years TidyByte: $0. Forever. Every feature included. Gemini Photos (when active): $47.98 over two years at $23.99/year. Gemini Photos lifetime: $35.99 one-time — now a sunk cost since the app is discontinued. For former Gemini Photos subscribers, the math is painful. Users who paid for a lifetime license received no refund when the app was discontinued. Annual subscribers lost access when their subscription expired. This is the inherent risk of subscription-based utility apps — if the developer decides to shut down, your investment disappears. Open-source tools like TidyByte do not carry this risk because the code is publicly available and the app has no dependency on a single company's servers or business decisions. If you were paying for Gemini Photos, switching to TidyByte saves you roughly $24 per year while giving you access to features like video compression and a storage dashboard that Gemini Photos never offered. Over five years, that is $120 saved — enough to upgrade your iCloud storage tier or contribute to a new phone fund. Privacy: On-Device vs. Cloud Processing When you hand a photo cleanup app access to your entire library, you are trusting it with some of the most personal data on your phone — family photos, medical documents, screenshots of private conversations. How each app handles that data matters enormously. TidyByte processes everything on-device. No photos are uploaded to any server. No usage analytics are collected. No tracking SDKs are embedded in the app. The only permission TidyByte requests is Photo Library access, and it uses that permission exclusively to read your photos, analyze them for duplicates and quality issues, and write deletion or album-sorting changes back to your library. Because TidyByte is open-source on GitHub , every network call (or lack thereof) can be independently verified. You can also read the full privacy policy for a plain-language breakdown. Gemini Photos, like most commercial apps from established companies, included analytics and crash-reporting SDKs. MacPaw's privacy policy disclosed the collection of device identifiers, usage patterns, and diagnostic data. While Gemini Photos did not upload your actual photos to the cloud for processing, the metadata it collected — how many photos you have, how often you clean them, what categories you delete most — painted a detailed picture of your behavior. This data was shared with third-party analytics providers as outlined in their privacy policy. For privacy-conscious users, the difference is clear. TidyByte's on-device-only architecture means your photos never leave your phone. The app works without an internet connection — useful on flights, in rural areas, or anywhere you want to clean your library without worrying about data transmission. There is no account to create, no email to provide, and no terms of service that grant the developer broad rights over your data. The code is open, the app is free, and your photos stay yours. Which One Should You Choose? The honest answer is that choosing between TidyByte and Gemini Photos is no longer a real decision. Gemini Photos is discontinued. It does not receive updates, it does not work reliably on current iOS versions, and it is no longer available for download. If you still have it installed, it is living on borrowed time — every iOS update risks breaking it further. But even when Gemini Photos was active, TidyByte offers a more complete feature set. Gemini Photos excelled at duplicate detection and had a beautifully designed interface. TidyByte matches those strengths and goes further with video compression, burst photo management, Live Photo conversion, a storage dashboard, and batch operations. The average TidyByte user reclaims 3 to 5 GB of storage in their first session — a figure that includes video compression savings that Gemini Photos could never provide. There are a few scenarios where you might consider other alternatives. If you need a macOS companion app to clean photos on your computer as well, MacPaw still sells CleanMyMac, which includes a photo cleanup module. If you want a cloud-based solution that works across devices, Google Photos offers storage management tools, though at the cost of uploading your entire library to Google's servers. For most iPhone users, though, an on-device tool is the right choice — and among those, TidyByte is the most feature-complete free option available. The long-term outlook also favors TidyByte. As an open-source project, it is not dependent on a single company's revenue targets or strategic pivots. The source code is publicly available, meaning the community can maintain and improve it even if the original developers move on. Gemini Photos' fate — abandoned without warning — is a cautionary tale about closed-source subscription apps. TidyByte's model eliminates that risk entirely. Migration Guide: Switching from Gemini Photos If you are coming from Gemini Photos, switching to TidyByte takes less than five minutes. There is no data to migrate because TidyByte reads directly from your iPhone's photo library — the same library Gemini Photos accessed. All your albums, favorites, and organizational structure remain intact. Here is a step-by-step guide to get started. Step 1: Download and grant access Download TidyByte from the App Store . When you first launch it, the app will request Photo Library access. Grant full access so TidyByte can scan your entire library. This permission stays on-device — TidyByte does not upload anything. You can verify this by monitoring network traffic or reviewing the open-source code . Step 2: Start with the storage dashboard Unlike Gemini Photos, which threw you straight into suggestions, TidyByte offers a storage dashboard that shows exactly where your space is going. Check this first — it will tell you how many duplicates you have, how many blurry photos are in your library, how much space your videos consume, and how many screenshots are taking up room. This overview helps you prioritize which cleanup task to tackle first. Step 3: Tackle duplicates and blurry photos Head to the duplicates section first, since this is what Gemini Photos users will find most familiar. TidyByte groups exact duplicates and near-duplicates separately, with the "best" version in each group pre-selected to keep. Review the groups, deselect any you want to preserve, and delete the rest. Then move to blurry photos — TidyByte scores each photo's sharpness and surfaces the worst ones for quick review. For most users, these two steps alone recover 1 to 3 GB of storage. Step 4: Compress videos and clean screenshots Gemini Photos never offered video compression, so this is a new opportunity for former users. Navigate to the video compression tool and let TidyByte analyze your video library. It will show you the current size of each video and the estimated size after compression. You can compress individual videos or batch-compress all of them. A typical user recovers 1 to 2 GB from video compression alone. After that, clean up screenshots — most people have hundreds of forgotten screenshots from months or years ago that serve no purpose. Step 5: Set up a maintenance routine Gemini Photos had a reminders feature that nudged you to clean up periodically. TidyByte works the same way — launch it once a month, spend 5 to 10 minutes swiping through recent photos, and your library stays under control. Because TidyByte is free with no subscription to manage, there is no reason not to keep it installed permanently as part of your iPhone maintenance toolkit. ## TidyByte vs Slidebox: Swipe Photo Cleaners Compared
URL: https://tidybyte.360ghar.com/blog/tidybyte-vs-slidebox

Skip to content TidyByte Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support Features Blog FAQ Changelog Support GitHub &rarr; Home / Blog / TidyByte vs Slidebox Comparison TidyByte vs Slidebox: Swipe Photo Cleaners Compared Published June 13, 2026 &middot; 7 min read If your iPhone is running low on storage, swipe-based photo cleaners offer the fastest way to sort through thousands of images. Two apps dominate this space: Slidebox, which has been around since 2017, and TidyByte, a newer free and open-source alternative. This TidyByte vs Slidebox comparison breaks down every feature, pricing model, and privacy practice so you can pick the right tool for your photo library. The average iPhone user has over 2,000 photos stored locally, and Apple estimates that screenshots, duplicates, and blurry shots account for roughly 30% of that total. A swipe cleaner lets you blast through that clutter in minutes rather than hours. But not all swipe cleaners are built the same — and the differences between TidyByte and Slidebox are significant. Swipe Interface Comparison Both TidyByte and Slidebox use a card-stack interface where you swipe left to delete and right to keep. This Tinder-style mechanic works because it reduces a complex decision (keep or trash) to a single gesture. You see one photo at a time, full-screen, which forces you to make a call without getting distracted by the rest of your library. Where they differ is in the details. Slidebox shows photos in chronological order with no filtering options — you simply start swiping from your camera roll and work forward or backward. TidyByte, on the other hand, lets you choose your starting point. You can begin with a specific album, filter by media type (photos, videos, screenshots, or Live Photos), or let the app surface the worst offenders first — blurry shots, duplicates, and large files — so you reclaim the most storage with the fewest swipes. TidyByte also adds a "Select All" function for categories like screenshots and duplicates, which lets you delete dozens of similar items in one tap instead of swiping through each one. Slidebox lacks any batch selection. For users with 5,000 or more photos, this single feature can save 20 to 30 minutes per cleanup session. Both apps support undo. In Slidebox, you shake your device to undo the last action. TidyByte provides an on-screen undo button plus a full session summary before any deletions are finalized, so you can review what you trashed before committing. This two-step confirmation prevents accidental deletions — a common complaint among Slidebox users in App Store reviews. Feature Comparison The feature gap between these two apps is where the TidyByte vs Slidebox comparison gets interesting. Slidebox focuses on one thing: swipe to sort photos into albums or trash. It does that job, but that is all it does. TidyByte is a full photo cleanup toolkit. Smart Cleaner Overview Smart Cleaner (sometimes listed as "Smart Cleaner: Clean Up Storage" on the App Store) is developed by AD26 Studio and positions itself as an all-in-one phone storage optimizer. The app offers duplicate photo detection, contact cleanup, calendar event management, and general storage analysis.
